title: Drug abuse and Kenya’s youth: A threat to lives and the economy
description: Substance abuse is quietly dismantling Kenya’s most valuable resource — and the response remains dangerously inadequate By Esther Wambui Kenya’s young people are the country’s most valuable asset — and drug and substance abuse is steadily destroying them. What begins as experimentation, peer pressure or an attempt to cope with stress can rapidly harden into dependence, derailing education, damaging health, fracturing relationships and stripping young people of the productive futures they were promised. The National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse has identified youth as among the most vulnerable groups in Kenya, confirming that this is not a private struggle but a national emergency with serious economic consequences. The scale of the problem demands an urgent, coordinated response. Schools and universities must strengthen drug education, expand counselling services and develop early-identification systems for students at risk. Parents and communities must create environments where young people can speak openly about stress, peer pressure and addiction without fear of stigma — because silence is where dependence takes root. Government agencies and health professionals must make treatment and rehabilitation services genuinely accessible, not merely available on paper to those with the means to reach them. Kenya cannot afford to treat this as a marginal concern. A generation lost to addiction is a generation of businesses not built, families not stabilised and national development stalled. Every young person who slips through the gaps in prevention and recovery represents not only a personal tragedy but a measurable economic cost the country will carry for years. Protecting Kenya’s youth from drug abuse is not charity. It is the most practical investment this country can make in its own future. title: Kenya’s Ebola battle: Is the country finally winning the fight against the deadly virus?
description: With its last patient discharged and a 42-day countdown begun, Kenya is closer than ever to an Ebola-free declaration — but the threat is far from over By Collins Kibet Kenya reached a landmark moment in its fight against Ebola yesterday when the country’s last patient undergoing treatment for the disease was discharged, triggering a critical 42-day monitoring period that, if passed without incident, will see the country officially declared Ebola-free on 23 December 2026. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale made the announcement at Afya House in Nairobi, bringing cautious relief to millions of Kenyans who have watched the outbreak unfold since the country confirmed its first case of Bundibugyo virus disease on 6 October 2026. That initial case involved a Kenyan national who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before developing symptoms — a reminder of how quickly infectious disease can cross borders in an interconnected region. The outbreak, which the World Health Organisation has been monitoring closely, eventually recorded nine confirmed cases. The initial patient infected four family members and four healthcare workers who had attended to him before Ebola was suspected. Two people died; seven recovered. All secondary infections were identified among individuals already in quarantine, a containment achievement that prevented the virus from reaching the wider community. Health authorities successfully traced and monitored 135 contacts linked to the initial case — a logistical undertaking that underscored the seriousness with which Kenya’s public health system responded. Yesterday’s discharge of the final patient also saw the last 11 contacts complete their monitoring period and return home in good health. Kenya today has no Ebola patients under treatment and no identified contacts in quarantine. The 42-day countdown, based on twice the longest recognised incubation period of the virus, began this morning and must run without a new infection before the declaration can be made. The WHO has praised Kenya’s response, recognising healthcare workers, government institutions and communities for containing an outbreak that, in less prepared circumstances, could have spiralled into a national crisis. Officials highlighted early detection, transparency, coordinated emergency operations and rigorous contact tracing as the pillars of an effective response. The outbreak demonstrated what is possible when public health institutions and ordinary citizens work in the same direction — a lesson worth recording for future reference. That future reference may come sooner than anyone would like. The situation in the DRC, the source of Kenya’s initial case, remains deeply alarming. The DRC has recorded more than 11,000 infections and over 5,000 deaths in its ongoing outbreak, according to the latest regional figures. Cross-border movement, commerce and international travel create continuous opportunities for the virus to migrate. Kenya’s last patient may have recovered, but the regional environment that produced this outbreak has not changed. The government has consequently maintained heightened surveillance, including screening at points of entry, community monitoring and rapid response capacity. The Ministry of Health has reminded the public to remain alert for symptoms — fever, weakness, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and unexplained bleeding — and to contact the toll-free number 719 at the first sign of concern. These measures are not precautionary theatre. They are essential disciplines that must hold for 42 more days and well beyond. The infection of four healthcare workers during the outbreak deserves particular attention. Medical professionals on the frontline of any infectious disease response face risks that the public rarely fully appreciates. Their exposure in this instance highlights the ongoing need for adequate protective equipment, rigorous infection prevention protocols, continuous training and sufficient medical resources at every level of the health system. Protecting healthcare workers is not merely an institutional obligation — it is a prerequisite for protecting everyone else. The outbreak has also exposed structural questions about Kenya’s broader preparedness for public health emergencies. The country managed to contain infections within a single transmission cluster, which is a genuine achievement. But the experience has revealed the importance of modern laboratory facilities in counties beyond Nairobi, trained emergency response personnel across regions and disease surveillance systems that do not depend on a centralised response from the capital. County governments must absorb this lesson and invest accordingly, particularly in areas where access to quality medical services remains limited. Public awareness must remain a central pillar of the strategy. Misinformation, fear and stigma are as dangerous in a health emergency as the pathogen itself. They discourage people from seeking care, undermine contact tracing and punish survivors who deserve support rather than discrimination. The government must continue providing accurate, accessible information through health facilities, schools, community leaders and credible media. Recovered patients must be welcomed back into their communities without reservation. Accountability matters too. The resources deployed during this emergency response — medical supplies, personnel, logistics and emergency funds — must be accounted for transparently. Public confidence in the health system is a long-term asset, and it is built or eroded by how institutions behave under pressure. The lessons from this outbreak should translate into lasting structural improvements, not temporary measures that fade once the emergency passes. Kenya has demonstrated something important during these weeks: that a coordinated, transparent and community-rooted response can contain a dangerous pathogen even in a country with real healthcare constraints. That is not a small achievement, and it should be recognised as such. But the celebration must wait. The coming 42 days will determine whether Kenya completes this chapter cleanly. Kenyans must remain vigilant, healthcare workers must continue receiving the support they have earned, and the government must sustain the discipline that brought the country to this point. The finish line is 23 December 2026. Kenya has come too far to stumble now. title: Education is the key to a brighter future
description: Kenya is sitting on its most powerful development tool — and consistently underfunding it By Pamela Aoko Education remains the most reliable path out of poverty, the foundation of economic growth and the engine of social progress — yet Kenya continues to treat it as a budget line rather than a national priority. The evidence for education’s transformative power is not in dispute. When individuals acquire knowledge, practical skills and professional qualifications, their employment prospects improve, their earning potential rises and their communities benefit. Multiply that across millions of young Kenyans and the national dividend is enormous. The question is not whether education matters — it is why the system designed to deliver it remains so chronically under-resourced. The challenges are well known and persistently unresolved: inadequate learning facilities, prohibitive costs for low-income families, insufficient teaching materials and deeply unequal access between urban and rural communities. These are not new problems. They are structural failures that successive governments have acknowledged and inadequately addressed. The remedies are equally well understood. Increased public funding for education, improved school infrastructure, the recruitment of qualified teachers in underserved areas and targeted scholarships for students from disadvantaged backgrounds would collectively transform outcomes. Parents must remain active partners in their children’s learning, and teachers must continue adopting methods that reach every student — not only the most prepared. None of this is complicated in principle. What it requires is political will and sustained financial commitment — both of which have too often fallen short. The future of every nation begins in a classroom. The quality of what happens inside that classroom determines everything that follows. title: Laikipia University: A centre of learning, opportunity and growth
description: Nestled in the highlands of Laikipia County, a quietly ambitious public university is producing graduates ready to compete By Naomi Andhamo Laikipia University, situated along the Nyahururu–Nakuru Highway in the heart of Laikipia County, is doing something that too few Kenyan institutions manage quietly well: preparing ordinary students for an increasingly competitive world. The university’s academic offer spans education, communication, science, technology, business and criminology — a breadth that lecturer Angeline Kwamboka says gives students genuine flexibility in shaping their career paths. She credits assignments, group discussions and research projects with building the independent thinking employers now demand. “Quality teaching and active student participation,” she says, “are essential in preparing learners for what lies ahead.” Students appear to agree. Charlotte Pearl describes her lecturers as approachable and genuinely invested in student success. She singles out group discussions and library facilities as particularly valuable — spaces where ideas are tested and knowledge deepened. The university’s cool highland climate, she adds with a smile, does not hurt concentration either. Student leader Michael Njoroge, who represents the School of Education, describes his role as a bridge between student concerns and university management — one that demands patience, empathy and the ability to hold competing opinions without losing sight of practical solutions. He notes that students facing financial pressure can access work opportunities within the institution, a small but meaningful safety net. Laikipia University will need to keep pace with the accelerating demands of digital skills and practical training. The foundations, however, are solid. For the students who walk through its gates each semester, the opportunity to learn, grow and move closer to their ambitions remains very much alive. title: Opposition leaders visit Gachagua to offer condolences after sister’s death
description: The Karen visits by Kalonzo, Matiang’i and their delegations carried the warmth of friendship — and the unmistakable undertone of 2027 By: Grace Wanja Senior opposition leaders, including Wiper Patriotic Front leader Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, yesterday visited former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua at his Karen home to offer condolences following the death of his elder sister, Eunice Nyangari Gachagua, who was 77. The visits, conducted separately but carrying a strikingly similar political undercurrent, brought together figures who have rarely shared the same platform — and who, until recently, occupied very different positions in Kenya’s shifting political landscape. That they converged on Gachagua’s home within the same week, each accompanied by senior party delegations, was noted by political observers as something more than a courtesy call. With Kenya’s general election now less than nine months away, the symbolism of solidarity was unmistakable. Kalonzo arrived with a delegation from the Wiper Patriotic Front that included Deputy Party Leader Mohamed Ali, Danson Mwashako, Eng. Thaddeus Nzambia, Musili Mawathe and Irene Kasalu. His condolence message was warm and deeply personal. “My brother Rigathi Gachagua, Reverend Dorcas Rigathi and the entire Gachagua family, be encouraged by the words of our Lord Jesus Christ in Matthew 5:4: ‘Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted,'” Kalonzo said. “May you find comfort in knowing that her 77 years of life were a blessing to her family and all who knew her.” Matiang’i arrived separately, accompanied by members of the Jubilee Party National Executive Committee. His message struck a tone of fraternal solidarity between men who have navigated Kenya’s brutal political terrain from different vantage points. “In moments of grief, the bonds of friendship, family and shared humanity remind us of the importance of standing with one another,” Matiang’i said. “We continue to hold the Gachagua family in our thoughts and prayers during this difficult time.” Among those in Matiang’i’s delegation was Geoffrey Mosiria, who is pursuing the Nairobi gubernatorial seat and who used the visit to signal his alignment with the emerging opposition constellation. Mosiria said Gachagua had personally encouraged him to press forward with his bid, framing the Nairobi race as part of a broader effort to dismantle what the opposition characterises as a failed administration. “I am committed to working closely with Gachagua, Matiang’i, Kalonzo and Senator Edwin Sifuna towards a common vision of reclaiming our country and restoring effective leadership in Nairobi,” Mosiria said. The language in those remarks — reclaiming, restoring, repossessing — is not grief language. It is campaign language, and its appearance in a condolence statement reflects the degree to which Kenyan political figures struggle, and perhaps no longer try, to separate the personal from the political. The visit was genuine. The grief expressed was real. But the conversation that reportedly accompanied it — about unity, shared purpose and the road to 2027 — was equally real, and arguably the more consequential part of the encounter. Gachagua’s political resurrection has been one of the more remarkable stories of the past year. Impeached as Deputy President in October 2024 in circumstances his supporters continue to contest, he has since built the Democracy for the Citizens Party, toured the Kenyan diaspora in the United States and cultivated relationships across a broad swathe of the opposition. His sister’s death has, in a painful irony, provided a moment of convergence that formal political summits rarely manage to produce. When leaders come to your home in sorrow, the conversations they have there tend to carry a different quality of candour. The political arithmetic being assembled around Gachagua is complex but increasingly legible. Kalonzo brings Ukambani and a national profile built over decades. Matiang’i brings credibility among the Kikuyu political establishment and a reformist reputation that survived the turbulence of the Kenyatta administration. Sifuna, whose name appeared in Mosiria’s remarks, anchors the formation’s connections into Western Kenya. Together, they represent a coalition that, if it holds, would present a formidable challenge to President William Ruto’s Broad-Based Government heading into August 2027. Whether it holds is the question that will define the next nine months of Kenyan politics. Opposition coalitions in this country have a well-documented tendency to fracture under the weight of competing presidential ambitions, constituency pressures and the perennial temptation of negotiated accommodation with the incumbent. Gachagua himself has not formally declared a presidential bid, though few serious political analysts doubt that one is coming. How the other figures in this emerging formation respond to that declaration, when it arrives, will reveal the true depth of the solidarity on display in Karen this week. For now, the family is grieving. Eunice Nyangari Gachagua, described by those who knew her as a woman whose life was a quiet blessing to her family and community, was buried with the kind of dignity her years deserved. Her brother, who has known extraordinary political turbulence in a short span of time, received the condolences of men who are simultaneously his allies, his rivals and his potential partners in what promises to be a defining electoral contest. In Kenya, the line between mourning and mobilising has always been thin. This week, it was thinner than most. title: Rising Stars strike late to sink Ivory Coast and edge closer to Olympics dream
description: Kenya’s Under-23 side produced a gritty second-half comeback at Nyayo to seize a crucial first-leg advantage in their Los Angeles 2028 qualifying campaign By Martin Weche Kenya’s Rising Stars delivered a dramatic late winner yesterday to beat Ivory Coast 2-1 in the first leg of their Olympic Games second-round qualifier at Nyayo National Stadium in Nairobi, keeping their Los Angeles 2028 dream firmly alive. It was the kind of victory that qualification campaigns are built on — scrappy, tense and ultimately decisive. For long stretches of a cagey encounter, the Rising Stars struggled to impose themselves on a well-organised Ivorian side, and a goalless first half did little to ease the anxiety of a home support that had arrived expecting fireworks. The second half, however, told a different story entirely. Kenya’s breakthrough came in the 65th minute through substitute Henry Omollo, whose introduction proved an inspired decision by the coaching staff. Omollo had been on the pitch only briefly when he found the net, sending Nyayo into a burst of noise that temporarily transformed the atmosphere inside the stadium. The lead, though, lasted just nine minutes. Oumar Konaté drew Ivory Coast level in the 74th minute with a finish that silenced the home crowd and shifted momentum sharply towards the visitors, who suddenly sensed an away draw that would serve them well heading into the second leg. What followed was a nervy final quarter that tested the character of a young Kenyan side under genuine pressure. The Rising Stars, to their considerable credit, did not retreat. They continued to press for a winner, and their persistence was rewarded six minutes from time when Andreas Odhiambo struck to restore Kenya’s lead and seal a 2-1 victory that significantly improves their prospects ahead of the return fixture in Abidjan on 17 November. The result gives Kenya a valuable cushion. Travelling to West Africa with a one-goal advantage is far from comfortable — Ivory Coast are an experienced and technically capable side who will be confident of reversing the deficit on home soil — but it is infinitely preferable to the alternative. A draw at Nyayo would have left the Rising Stars needing to win away from home simply to advance; now they carry momentum, a lead and the psychological boost of having come from behind to win. The stakes extend well beyond a single tie. This qualification campaign serves simultaneously as the pathway to the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations Under-23 tournament, meaning every match carries double significance for Kenya’s emerging generation of footballers. Should the Rising Stars navigate past Ivory Coast in Abidjan, they will advance to the third round of Olympic qualifying, where either Gabon or Tunisia await in March next year. That would represent a significant achievement for a programme that has been building steadily and now finds itself within reach of a genuinely historic qualification. Odhiambo’s late strike will inevitably attract the headlines, and rightly so — it was a goal that required both technical composure and the mental fortitude to deliver in a high-pressure moment. But the more significant story is the collective resilience the Rising Stars showed after conceding the equaliser. Lesser sides, particularly at Under-23 level, buckle when a lead disappears. This group pressed on. The job, of course, is only half done. Nyayo provided the platform; Abidjan will provide the examination. Ivory Coast at home, with a crowd behind them and a deficit to erase, will be a markedly different proposition from the side that left Nairobi yesterday evening on the wrong end of the scoreline. Kenya’s Rising Stars have earned the right to dream. Whether that dream survives the return leg on Monday will depend on whether this performance was a statement of intent or simply a good night’s work. title: The theatre of déjà vu: Pochettino dreams again at Old Trafford
description: Mauricio Pochettino is closing in on the Manchester United job — but rescuing a club in freefall demands more than a dream appointment By Andalo Christine Ingutia Manchester United are closing in on the appointment of Mauricio Pochettino as their next head coach, with the Argentine reported to have reached a verbal agreement in principle with the club as Michael Carrick’s position hangs by a thread. Reports by The Athletic and Sky Sports yesterday confirmed that United have agreed personal terms with Pochettino, placing him firmly in pole position to take charge at Old Trafford should the club’s leadership decide to remove Carrick. That decision is expected to emerge from a crunch meeting between senior executives, including chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco — a gathering that speaks volumes about the gravity of United’s predicament. The numbers tell a grim story. United sit 18th in the Premier League after winning just one of their opening ten matches — their worst start to a top-flight season in 40 years. While the hierarchy deliberated in Monaco, Carrick continued taking training at Carrington yesterday morning, outwardly composed as he awaited a verdict on his future. Pochettino’s appointment would represent a significant statement of intent from a club that has admired the Argentine for years. His Premier League credentials are well established: he transformed Southampton into an attacking force before guiding Tottenham Hotspur to the 2019 UEFA Champions League final and a second-place Premier League finish. He subsequently won Ligue 1 with Paris Saint-Germain and steadied a chaotic Chelsea project, overseeing a markedly improved second half of the 2023/24 season. His reputation for developing young players and building cohesive, attacking teams makes him a compelling fit for a club that badly needs both. The complications, however, are considerable. Pochettino extended his contract with the United States men’s national team in August, committing to the programme through the 2030 World Cup. Prising him away will require a release fee of approximately £7 million, plus potential compensation for members of his coaching staff. United are reportedly working to finalise arrangements in time for their Premier League trip to Anfield on 22 November — a fixture that would represent either a baptism of fire or a statement of renewed purpose, depending on one’s appetite for symbolism. In the meantime, Pochettino is focused on preparing the United States for their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on 14 and 18 November. His professionalism in honouring those commitments while United’s approach is confirmed reflects a manager who understands the weight of his obligations — a quality Old Trafford has not always been fortunate enough to attract in recent years. The romance of the association between Pochettino and United is real. He has long been linked with the job, and there is genuine excitement among supporters at the prospect of a manager with his track record finally arriving. But the circumstances of this appointment carry none of the comfort of a fresh start. United are not recruiting from a position of strength — they are reaching for a lifeline from the relegation zone, and whoever takes charge will need results immediately, not the runway to build gradually. Pochettino has experience of pressure, of rebuilding, and of galvanising a squad that has lost its way. Whether those qualities are sufficient to rescue a club this dysfunctional, in a league this unforgiving, is a question only the pitch can answer. Until United make an official announcement, the appointment remains conditional. But the direction of travel is clear. A decade-long association between the Argentine and Old Trafford may finally be nearing its conclusion — for better or worse, the moment is arriving. title: MPs pass Bill to end hospital detention of patients and bodies over unpaid bills
description: Kenya’s National Assembly has moved to close a legal gap that has left discharged patients trapped and bereaved families unable to bury their dead By James Mwangi The National Assembly yesterday passed a Bill prohibiting hospitals from detaining discharged patients or withholding the bodies of deceased persons over unpaid medical bills, sending the proposed legislation to the Senate for consideration before it proceeds to President William Ruto for assent. The Bill, sponsored by Kirinyaga Woman Representative Njeri Maina, addresses a practice that has persisted in Kenyan hospitals for years, exploiting the absence of explicit statutory prohibition to hold patients and corpses as effective collateral against outstanding treatment costs. For families already navigating grief or medical crisis, the additional burden of negotiating a loved one’s release — from a ward or a morgue — has long been one of the more quietly devastating features of Kenya’s healthcare system. Maina and the lawmakers who backed the Bill argued during debate that hospitals have continued to operate in a legislative grey zone, using gaps in existing law to justify detentions that courts have repeatedly found unacceptable. Several rulings by Kenyan courts have held that the detention of patients and bodies over unpaid bills violates constitutional rights, yet without a clear statutory framework, the practice has continued, with individual cases requiring individual legal battles that most affected families cannot afford to fight. The proposed law would change that fundamentally. Under its provisions, a hospital would be explicitly prohibited from detaining any patient who has been medically cleared for discharge, regardless of whether their bill has been settled. It would equally bar the withholding of a deceased person’s remains over outstanding medical expenses — a practice that has, in documented cases, left families unable to hold funerals for weeks or months while financial negotiations dragged on. The human cost behind these cases is not abstract. Across Kenya, families have faced the specific anguish of a loved one dying in hospital, only to find that grief must be deferred until money is found. Children have been detained in maternity wards alongside their mothers. Elderly patients, medically fit to leave, have remained in beds they no longer need because discharge was contingent on payment. The Bill’s passage through the National Assembly represents a direct legislative response to that accumulated harm. National Assembly Health Committee Chairperson James Nyikal supported the Bill’s intent while introducing a broader structural argument. Nyikal maintained that while the legislation was necessary, the more durable solution lay in Kenyans consistently contributing to the Social Health Authority scheme. “Sustained contributions to SHA would help address the financial challenges that leave patients and families unable to settle hospital bills in the first place,” he said — a position that locates the detention problem within the larger failure of health financing rather than treating it as an isolated institutional misbehaviour. Nyikal’s point carries weight. The practice of detaining patients and bodies is, in most cases, a symptom of a system in which hospitals — particularly private and mission facilities operating on thin margins — carry significant unpaid debt from patients who genuinely cannot afford their bills. Outlawing detention removes one harmful response to that problem without resolving the underlying financial gap. The SHA, launched as the successor to the National Health Insurance Fund, is intended to provide that resolution by spreading health costs across a broader contribution base. Its success in doing so remains, at this stage, an open question. The Bill now moves to the Senate, where it will face scrutiny from a chamber that has in recent sessions engaged substantively with health legislation. If the Senate passes the Bill without amendments, it proceeds directly to the President for assent. If amendments are introduced, the two chambers will need to reconcile their versions — a process that can extend the legislative timeline considerably. The timeline to enactment therefore remains uncertain, though the National Assembly’s passage of the Bill represents the most significant legislative progress on this issue to date. The broader political context matters too. Kenya’s healthcare system has been under sustained public scrutiny since the transition from NHIF to SHA, a process marked by implementation difficulties, provider disputes and public anxiety about coverage gaps. The government has faced criticism from medical professionals, patients’ advocates and opposition politicians over the pace and quality of the transition. The passage of this Bill offers the legislature an opportunity to demonstrate responsiveness to a healthcare grievance that cuts across political and class lines — the detention of bodies and patients is not a problem that affects only the poor, though it falls most heavily on those with the least capacity to resolve it quickly. For Maina, the Bill’s passage is a legislative achievement that speaks directly to constituents in Kirinyaga and, by extension, to families across the country who have experienced or fear this particular form of institutional pressure. Kirinyaga, like many counties, has hospitals — public and private — where the practice has occurred, and the Woman Representative’s decision to bring the legislation reflects both local experience and national relevance. What the Bill does not resolve, it at least makes visible. By establishing an explicit statutory prohibition, it creates a legal standard against which hospitals can be held accountable, and it gives patients and families a clearer basis for seeking redress when that standard is violated. Enforcement will depend on the commitment of regulatory bodies and the courts, but a law on the books is a materially different instrument than a court ruling that must be relitigated case by case. Kenya has long debated the right to health as a constitutional guarantee. The National Assembly’s vote yesterday brought that guarantee one step closer to practical meaning — at least for those who have ever stood in a hospital corridor, grief in hand, waiting for permission to take their people home. The Senate now holds the next decision. It should not take long. The post MPs pass Bill to end hospital detention of patients and bodies over unpaid bills appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Sifuna warns youth: Re-elect Ruto and lose your political future
description: The Linda Mwananchi Movement is expanding into Laikipia with a sharp message for young Kenyans — and a direct challenge to the president ahead of 2027 By James Mwangi Linda Mwananchi Movement party leader Edwin Sifuna yesterday warned young Kenyans that re-electing President William Ruto in 2027 would foreclose their prospects of ascending to leadership positions by 2032, as his party received defectors from the Orange Democratic Movement at a press conference in Laikipia County. The event marked a visible expansion of the movement’s organisational footprint into a county that has historically been contested political territory, and Sifuna used the platform to sharpen his party’s pitch to younger voters — the demographic that proved decisive during the 2022 general election and that every major political formation is now actively courting ahead of August 2027. “I want to tell all young people: if you elect Ruto again, no young person will be a leader in 2032,” Sifuna said, delivering the message in a register designed to land with an audience that has grown increasingly vocal about political exclusion and generational change. The warning was blunt by design. With Kenya’s youth bulge well documented — the majority of registered voters are under 35 — the question of who controls the youth vote is, in practical terms, the question of who wins the next election. Sifuna’s critique extended beyond the presidential race. He singled out the long-delayed Nanyuki-Doldol road project in Laikipia County as a symbol of what he characterised as a pattern of unfulfilled development promises. “We have heard about the road from Nanyuki to Doldol for many years. Stop talking to Ruto about it — I will come and build it myself,” he said, a pledge that drew applause from the gathering but will inevitably invite scrutiny as the campaign period intensifies and promises require costing. His most pointed remark, however, was not about roads. “If you are not alive, even the Doldol road being built will not help you,” Sifuna said, a line that situated infrastructure promises within a broader argument about personal safety and the relationship between citizens and the state — a theme that has gained political traction in the wake of public protests and the controversies they generated. Sifuna also announced plans to visit Laikipia County formally as part of a wider effort to demonstrate LMM’s growing organisational strength. “We will come to Laikipia to show that our party is firm,” he said — a signal that the movement intends to treat the county as a genuinely competitive battleground rather than peripheral territory. The press conference featured contributions from the movement’s senior leadership, each carrying a distinct message aimed at different segments of the audience. Deputy Party Leader Faith Odhiambo addressed young people directly, framing LMM’s emergence as a generational moment. “Youth, our time is now. We are telling this government: we will not allow young people to be killed by the state,” she said, connecting the movement’s appeal to anxieties that have been building among younger Kenyans since the mid-2024 protests. Deputy Party Leader Kawira Mwangaza, the former Meru Governor, focused on the party’s electoral machinery, announcing that LMM intends to field candidates across all counties in 2027. “As Linda Mwananchi, we will field candidates everywhere in Kenya. Nominations will be free and fair,” she said — a commitment that, if delivered, would transform LMM from a pressure movement into a full-spectrum electoral vehicle capable of contesting parliamentary and civic seats alongside the presidency. Mwangaza also praised Sifuna’s personal integrity, describing him as “Mr Clean” — a characterisation that positions him against a political culture widely perceived as transactional and that echoes the kind of branding that has historically resonated with urban, educated and younger voters frustrated by establishment politics. LMM Secretary General Caroli Omondi went further, explicitly linking Sifuna to the political legacy of former Prime Minister Raila Odinga, who remains one of the most consequential figures in Kenya’s post-independence political history. “This Sifuna is the one who carries the spirit of Baba now. Do not be afraid. We are the ones who will protect you,” Omondi said — a framing that seeks to inherit the emotional and organisational loyalty that Odinga commanded across Western Kenya and parts of Nairobi without requiring Odinga’s direct endorsement. That inheritance claim is significant and contested. Odinga’s political network, built over decades and anchored in Luo Nyanza, does not transfer automatically, and several formations are positioning themselves as its natural successors. Sifuna’s advantage is that he brings both geographical roots — his networks span Luo Nyanza and Western Kenya — and a public profile sharpened through years as ODM Secretary General, a role that gave him direct experience of how national party machinery operates. His departure from ODM, and the defections the movement received yesterday, suggest that at least some of that network is following him. The Laikipia event is part of a broader pattern. Across Kenya’s political landscape, parties and movements are using the period between now and the official campaign season to build structures, recruit defectors and establish territorial presence. LMM’s move into Laikipia — a county with a mixed ethnic composition and a history of land-related political tension — suggests the movement is thinking beyond its perceived Western Kenya base. Whether that expansion translates into electoral results will depend on factors that press conferences cannot resolve: candidate quality, financial resources, coalition agreements and the final shape of the opposition’s presidential architecture. The question of who the opposition fields as its presidential candidate, and on what terms the other formations align behind that choice, remains the defining unresolved question of Kenya’s pre-election period. Sifuna has made his position clear. The youth, he argues, are the story of 2027 — and their choices will determine not just who wins, but who gets to lead Kenya in the decade that follows. The young people of Laikipia were listening. Whether they act on what they heard is the question that will only be answered at the ballot. title: Uhuru tells opposition: Unite or step aside as Kenya’s 2027 battle takes shape
description: At a Nairobi funeral, Kenya’s former president delivered his clearest signal yet that the opposition must consolidate — or concede the election before it begins By David Kimani Former President Uhuru Kenyatta yesterday used the funeral service of Beatrice Wambui Muturi at PCEA Nairobi West to deliver his most direct public message to opposition leaders yet, urging Rigathi Gachagua, Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka, Eugene Wamalwa and others to set aside personal ambitions and present a united front ahead of the August 2027 general election. The occasion carried the particular weight that Kenyan funerals often do — a convergence of grief and politics, of personal history and public calculation. Wambui, described by those present as a towering figure in both family and national political circles, had been close to Kenyatta’s mother, Mama Ngina, since her marriage to founding President Jomo Kenyatta. “She welcomed her into my father’s home when she got married to my father, and our extended family has lost one of its greatest pillars,” Kenyatta said in tribute. But the former president’s most consequential remarks were directed not at the departed, but at the living — and specifically at the men seated around him who harbour varying degrees of presidential ambition. “What happened in the past is in the past. What should concern Kenyans is where we are going,” Kenyatta said, before addressing Gachagua, Kalonzo and Wamalwa by name. “As I keep telling my brothers here — Steve, Rigathi, Eugene and others — only one person can occupy the presidency at a time. I also listen to the ground; my ears are not closed.” He said ordinary Kenyans, encountered during his own movements across the country, were sending an unambiguous message. “People want to see our leaders stand together. Our leaders must organise themselves and unite to fulfil what Kenyans want.” Kenyatta’s intervention is significant for several reasons. Having largely withdrawn from front-line politics since leaving office, he has re-entered the public conversation at a moment when the opposition landscape remains fluid and the question of who will carry a unified challenge to President William Ruto remains unresolved. His framing — that unity is a public demand, not a political favour — gives the message a popular legitimacy that a purely partisan call would lack. “And I am sure that is what you will deliver for us, with justice. There can be no peace without justice,” he added. The event also produced one of the more candid exchanges in recent Kenyan political memory. Gachagua, speaking ahead of Kenyatta, made a remarkable public admission: that he had spent KSh1.5 million given to him by Wambui to support Kenyatta’s 2017 repeat presidential campaign on personal needs. “When our election was nullified by the Supreme Court in 2017, we were so disappointed and did not even have money. She found me and gave me money in a nylon bag to help Uhuru win the repeat election — but I had my own needs. That KSh1.5 million, I confess, I spent on myself,” he said, to audible reaction from those gathered. Kenyatta’s response was characteristically dry. “I have retired, but I will go to Wamunyoro to claim my campaign money back,” he said, drawing laughter and underscoring the renewed warmth between two men whose relationship had visibly strained during the final turbulent period of the Jubilee administration. Gachagua was equally direct about the reconciliation. Recounting how he and Wambui had worked together to support Kenyatta’s first presidential bid, he said their relationship had subsequently been damaged by third parties. “Together with her, we worked to make Uhuru Kenyatta president during his first attempt. Someone came between me and Uhuru to divide us — but are we not together now?” he said. “Let me say this: nobody will ever succeed in coming between me and former President Uhuru Kenyatta again.” The DCP leader also employed an extended allegory — speaking in Kikuyu — involving a herder, a hyena and missing sheep, a thinly veiled reflection on his removal from the Deputy Presidency and what he characterised as a failure of oversight that allowed harm to occur. He asked, pointedly, whether he would receive support in addressing the problem without destroying what remained. The allegory drew nods and murmurs from an audience that understood its political architecture precisely. Kalonzo, for his part, struck a tone that balanced personal tribute with political assertion. He defended Kenyatta’s continued presence in national discourse, noting that retirement from office did not extinguish the right to political opinion. “We wanted Uhuru to stay out of this as we transform the country, but he is entitled to his opinion and still has the right to contribute to national discourse,” Kalonzo said. The Wiper leader also addressed the political energy among younger Kenyans directly, criticising remarks attributed to those in government that advocated shooting protesters. “When somebody says, ‘Shoot Gen Z in the leg,’ that is a presidential fear. This is why Kenyans are united in calling for one term. Young Kenyans have the right to express their political opinions. Next year, they will go to the ballot and say: you wanted to shoot us in the legs — we will shoot you at the ballot.” The gathering at PCEA Nairobi West was, on the surface, a farewell to a woman who had lived at the intersection of Kenya’s founding generation and its contemporary politics. Wambui had, by multiple accounts, been a quiet but consequential presence — supporting campaigns, facilitating connections and maintaining relationships across the political spectrum with a discretion that formal political figures rarely manage. But the conversations her funeral hosted were anything but quiet. With nine months to the election, every public gathering of this magnitude carries a subtext, and yesterday’s was not particularly sub. title: Renowned Tiktoker and self-proclaimed forex trader, KING TIZIAN, called out for living lavishly online while his grandmother’s body is detained at the mortuary over Ksh 150,000 bill
description: Thursday, November 12, 2026 - Popular TikToker and self-proclaimed forex trader King Tizian is facing criticism after it emerged that his grandmother’s body has been detained at a mortuary over an outstanding bill of KSh150,000, even as he continues to flaunt a lavish lifestyle on social media. According to a source, Tizian’s grandmother’s body has been stuck at the morgue after the family reportedly failed to raise the amount required to secure its release for burial. Reacting to the reports, Tizian confirmed that his grandmother’s body had indeed been detained over the unpaid mortuary bill. However, he lamented that some of his relatives and close family members expected him to clear the entire bill single-handedly simply because he is a celebrity who regularly displays opulence online. Tizian insisted that all family members should contribute towards settling the bill, arguing that his flashy social media lifestyle did not mean he had idle money lying around to cater for every family expense. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

description: Thursday, November 12, 2026 - Police officers have arrested a woman and recovered suspected narcotic drugs worth KSh459,000 during an intelligence-led operation in Kanduyi, Bungoma County. The operation was conducted at a residential house following intelligence reports, with officers raiding the premises and conducting a thorough search. During the operation, police discovered 15.3 kilogrammes of suspected narcotic substances concealed in different sections of the house. Officers also recovered KSh5,911 in cash, suspected to be proceeds of crime, alongside several materials believed to have been used in packaging and distributing the drugs. recovered substances, estimated to have a street value of KSh459,000, were secured as exhibits to support further investigations. female suspect was arrested and escorted to Bungoma Police Station, where she was placed in custody pending arraignment in court. National Police Service commended the officers involved for their vigilance and commitment to fighting drug trafficking, while also appreciating members of the public whose information continues to assist security agencies in dismantling criminal networks. arrest is part of ongoing efforts by the police to combat the distribution of narcotics and other criminal activities across the country. title: BABU OWINO cries foul as he questions why fellow Luos are fighting his 2027 Nairobi Governor bid - “I am your son”
description: Thursday, November 12, 2026 - Embakasi East MP Babu Owino has expressed frustration over what he described as growing opposition to his 2027 Nairobi governor bid within his own Luo community. Speaking during an interview with Ramogi TV conducted in Dholuo, the outspoken legislator claimed that he had attracted support from nearly every region in the country but was disappointed that some members of his community were working against his political aspirations. Babu, who has positioned himself within the opposition camp, argued that Nairobi politics was largely influenced by opposition politics, adding that leaders and supporters from different communities had rallied behind his gubernatorial ambitions. "Almost everyone in the opposition is supporting me. However, my own Luo community is still opposing me. “Why are you fighting me when I am your son? What have I done wrong? “Why are you against me?" he posed. The MP also addressed questions surrounding his Luo identity, claiming that some critics had questioned his ethnic background because of his light complexion, with others joking that he originated from Mumbai, India. He dismissed the claims, insisting that he was born and raised in Nyalenda slums in Kisumu, where he spent his formative years. The legislator also reminded his critics of his contribution to ODM and former Prime Minister Raila Odinga's presidential campaigns, recounting how he risked his life while traversing more than 280 constituencies to mobilise support for the party's presidential ambitions. Babu wondered why a community that previously celebrated his loyalty and political sacrifices was now seemingly turning against him. "I am still the same Babu you have always known. “I am your son, and I want you to look at me positively. “Do not oppose me just to make other people happy," he appealed. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Inside job? How a man was robbed of Ksh 950,000 after withdrawing the money from DTB Bank TRM branch
description: Thursday, November 12, 2026 - Detectives have launched investigations after a Nairobi resident lost KSh950,000 in a daring daylight robbery shortly after withdrawing the money from DTB Bank's TRM Mall branch. According to an OB report, the victim, a resident of Kiambu, had withdrawn the cash from the bank on Tuesday before driving to a car garage in Ridgeways. He reportedly parked his Toyota Prado along the road before entering the garage to check on another vehicle that was undergoing repairs. However, while inside the premises, he was alerted that someone had broken into his parked vehicle. He rushed outside and reportedly spotted a white saloon car being driven away from the scene. Upon inspecting his Prado, he discovered that the left passenger-side window had been smashed and the KSh950,000 he had withdrawn from the bank was missing. Police officers visited the scene and commenced investigations into the incident. The circumstances surrounding the robbery have raised questions about whether the victim was trailed from the bank or whether the suspects had prior knowledge that he was carrying a substantial amount of cash. In a public appeal, detectives called on anyone with relevant information to assist with the investigation. They particularly urged the bank to provide CCTV footage that could help establish what happened during and after the cash withdrawal. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Towards a successful future: Personal development as today’s most important investment
description: By: Nozanin Bahodirova When does a person’s future begin? Perhaps on the day they dream big? Or when they make an important decision in life? In reality, a successful future begins today, with the choices we make and the small steps we take right now. The world is changing faster than ever before. The knowledge that was sufficient yesterday may not be enough today, and professions that are in high demand now may require entirely new skills tomorrow. In such circumstances, people cannot afford to stand still. They must continue learning, exploring, thinking and, most importantly, working on themselves. Personal development is not simply about reading books, attending courses or acquiring new knowledge. Above all, it is about understanding oneself, discovering one’s potential, recognising one’s weaknesses and striving to become a better person than one was yesterday. Real change begins when people stop being indifferent to their lives and take responsibility for improving them. Dreaming is not enough — action is necessary. Every person has dreams, plans they wish to achieve and goals they hope to reach. However, there is a considerable distance between a dream and its fulfilment. This distance can only be covered through discipline, patience, hard work and determination. A life without goals is like a journey without direction. When people do not know where they are going, their efforts may not lead to the desired results. Therefore, we should set clear goals, plan how to achieve them and take at least one small step towards them every day. Of course, difficulties, failures and unexpected obstacles may appear along the way. However, these challenges do not necessarily mean that our abilities are limited. Instead, they may indicate that we need to gain new experience. Psychologist Albert Bandura emphasised that people’s beliefs in their own abilities influence their actions and achievements. Therefore, self-confidence is one of the important steps towards success. Knowledge is the key that opens the doors to the future. In modern society, being knowledgeable is a valuable asset. However, being willing to learn is even more important. True progress is closely connected to a person’s desire to acquire new knowledge. Reading books, learning foreign languages, improving professional skills and exploring new technologies all contribute to broadening one’s horizons. In particular, independent learning and the pursuit of personal interests can create greater opportunities for young people in the future. Nobody can increase our knowledge on our behalf. A teacher can guide us, books can provide information and courses can introduce new opportunities. However, genuine enthusiasm for learning must come from within. Time is an opportunity that cannot be regained. People often say that they do not have enough opportunities to achieve their dreams. In reality, however, the problem is sometimes not the lack of opportunities but how we use the time available to us. Small tasks completed throughout the day, a few pages of a book read, new words learned or a skill developed can lead to remarkable results over time. To achieve this, we must value our time, prioritise important tasks and reduce unnecessary distractions. In his work, Stephen Covey highlights the importance of setting priorities in order to lead an effective life. Indeed, being busy does not always mean being productive. What matters is spending our time on activities that bring us closer to our goals. Change does not begin with external circumstances; it begins with an internal decision. A person’s attitude towards themselves and their abilities determines the direction of their development. Sometimes, people consider their abilities unchangeable and hesitate to try new things. However, abilities and skills can be developed through effort, experience and education. Psychologist Carol Dweck demonstrates the importance of a growth mindset in acquiring new knowledge and overcoming challenges. This means that something we do not know today can be learned tomorrow, and a task we cannot accomplish today may become possible after gaining experience. Therefore, instead of constantly comparing ourselves with others, it is more beneficial to compare our present achievements with our previous progress. Everyone has their own path, opportunities and pace of development. Personal development is not only for yourself. The achievements of a person who continuously works on themselves are not limited to their personal life. Knowledgeable, responsible, proactive and independent-minded individuals can also contribute to the development of their families, communities and countries. In particular, the younger generation’s commitment to education, willingness to introduce new ideas, interest in international experiences and desire to demonstrate their potential are essential for future progress. UNESCO also recognises education as an important force in shaping the common future of humanity. Thus, personal development is not merely a means of achieving individual success; it is also a value that benefits society as a whole. In conclusion Nobody else will build a successful future for us. We create it ourselves through the knowledge we acquire, the decisions we make, the ambitions we pursue and the actions we take today. We do not have to accomplish extraordinary things every day. Sometimes, reading a single page of a book, gaining one new piece of knowledge, making a small but courageous decision or completing a task on time can become the beginning of significant changes. Most importantly, we must never lose confidence in ourselves, appreciate our opportunities and continue developing. After all, the future is not simply a time to be awaited. It is an opportunity to be created today. A person who works on themselves today is someone who cares about their tomorrow. title: Belt and Road think tank cooperation, int’l communication forums start in China’s Xi’an
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia XI’AN, Nov. (Xinhua) — The Belt and Road Forum for International Think Tank Cooperation 2026 and the 4th Silk Road (Xi’an) International Communication Forum opened in Xi’an, capital city of northwest China’s Shaanxi Province, on Tuesday. Themed “High-quality Belt and Road Cooperation Empowering Modernization and Mutual Learning among Civilizations,” these forums aim to pool global wisdom and promote new development of Belt and Road cooperation with higher quality and at a higher level. More than 300 diplomats, think tank experts, journalists, cultural and tourism experts, and business representatives from over 50 countries and regions are attending these forums to engage in exchanges and discussions. In his address, Zhao Gang, deputy secretary of the Shaanxi Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and governor of Shaanxi, said Shaanxi has in recent years deeply integrated itself into the broader pattern of Belt and Road cooperation. Lyu Yansong, editor-in-chief of Xinhua News Agency, said that over the past 13 years, Belt and Road cooperation has grown from a vision into tangible and visible cooperation projects, making positive contributions to enhancing friendship between China and partner countries and promoting the economic and social development of partner countries. As the lead of the Initiators Council of the Belt and Road Studies Network (BRSN), Xinhua is ready to work with domestic and international colleagues to deepen research and interpretation of the connotations of high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, showcase the fruitful achievements of partner countries in advancing modernization and mutual learning among civilizations, and gather strong momentum for high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, Lyu said. The BRSN has continued to expand its influence since its establishment seven years ago. At the opening ceremony, four new member institutions, namely BRICS International Forum, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Manas National Academy of the Kyrgyz Republic, and the Development Strategy Centre, Uzbekistan were presented with signing documents. A think tank report titled “Building an Open World Economy Through Belt and Road Cooperation” was, meanwhile, released globally in both Chinese and English. The forums are co-hosted by Xinhua News Agency, the CPC Shaanxi Provincial Committee and the Shaanxi Provincial People’s Government. ■ The post Belt and Road think tank cooperation, int’l communication forums start in China’s Xi’an appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Nyeri’s wage bill is eating our future
description: Nyeri County spends KSh 52 of every KSh 100 it receives on salaries — 17 percentage points above the legal limit — and the gap is costing residents roads, water, and health services. By Dr Grace Njine Nyeri County’s wage bill consumed 52 per cent of its total revenue last financial year — nearly double what the law allows and the highest proportion recorded among all 47 counties in Kenya. That figure is not contested. It comes from the county’s own County Budget Review and Outlook Paper 2026, which shows that by the end of FY 2025/26, Nyeri had spent KSh4.62B on salaries and allowances — 58.63 per cent of everything it actually spent that year. The Public Finance Management Act caps the wage bill at 35 per cent of county revenue. Nyeri is 17 points over that line. The scale of the problem becomes clearer when set against neighbours. The Controller of Budget’s review of all 47 counties for FY 2024/25 placed Nyeri at the top of the wage bill table at 55 per cent, ahead of Machakos and Baringo. In the same period, Murang’a spent 48 per cent of revenue on salaries, Embu 43 per cent, and Kiambu 42 per cent. Nyandarua held within the legal limit at 33 per cent. Kirinyaga’s trajectory is the most instructive comparison. In 2017/18, Kirinyaga spent 45 per cent of revenue on wages — worse than Nyeri is today. By FY 2025/26, the Salaries and Remuneration Commission ranked it among only five nationally compliant counties at 32 per cent. It achieved that by freezing recruitment, introducing performance incentives for revenue collectors, and growing its own-source revenue from approximately KSh300 million to KSh700 million. If Kirinyaga, working from a smaller economic base, can get under the line, so can Nyeri. The human cost of non-compliance is not abstract. Every shilling spent above the legal wage-bill ceiling is a shilling unavailable for roads, water infrastructure, dispensaries, coffee factories, and bursaries. If Nyeri brought its wage bill to 35 per cent, approximately KSh1.5B annually would be freed for development and services. That calculation is straightforward: the numbers are in the county’s own budget papers. This is not an argument against county workers. Nyeri’s nurses, agricultural extension officers, and ward administrators do essential work, frequently under difficult conditions. The problem lies in the structure of the payroll, not the people on it. How did Nyeri arrive here? There is no single cause and no single administration to blame. When devolution began in 2013, Nyeri inherited staff from former local authorities and from national government. By 2023, the county acknowledged to the Senate that many of those inherited employees lacked the technical skills required, forcing it to recruit new staff while retaining the old. Collective bargaining agreements and national salary reviews have repeatedly landed additional wage obligations on county budgets without matching transfers from the national government. Health workers alone account for 56 per cent of Nyeri’s wage bill, one of the highest proportions in the country. Payroll controls have also been weak: the Controller of Budget found Nyeri paying KSh109.65M in salaries outside the official payroll system in a single quarter — the kind of shadow payroll where ghost workers and irregular payments are hardest to detect. The county took a meaningful step in August 2026 by launching a payroll and personnel audit. The question is what follows. Audits matter only when they produce binding action. Neighbouring counties offer a practical map. Nyandarua conducted repeated physical headcounts and ordered staff found drawing double salaries to refund the money. Uasin Gishu now runs its entire payroll through the official system with no manual payments at all. Makueni links every department’s performance contract to staff appraisal, with both rewards and sanctions attached. These are replicable, proven approaches — not untested theory. For Nyeri, five steps are achievable within the current political term. First, complete and publish the payroll audit, follow it immediately with a biometric headcount, and set a firm target of zero manual payroll within twelve months. Second, establish an approved staff establishment for every department and freeze all hiring above it, except for critical health and technical positions. Third, reduce numbers humanely through natural attrition and redeployment rather than mass dismissals — Kirinyaga’s abrupt layoff of casual health workers in 2020 threw its hospitals into crisis and stands as a warning. Fourth, grow revenue: Nyeri’s hospitals, public markets, and county assets have unrealised earning potential, and every additional shilling of own-source revenue reduces the wage-bill ratio without cutting a single job. Fifth, extend performance contracts from the executive level down to ward administrators, and tie promotions and training allocations to measurable results. The law gives counties until June 2028 to reach the 35 per cent threshold. That deadline falls squarely within the term of whoever Nyeri voters elect in August 2027. The wage bill should therefore be a defining question of that election. When candidates come canvassing for votes, residents have one question that cuts through every promise: what is your specific, costed plan to bring the wage bill within the law? The answer — or the absence of one — will reveal more about an aspirant’s preparedness to govern than any campaign rally. Nyeri’s future is being consumed by its payroll. The county cannot develop what it cannot afford to build. Dr Grace Njine, CHRP(K), PMP, is a Human Resource Management and Public Service Reform specialist. She holds a PhD in Human Resource Management from Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and an MBA from the University of Nairobi. She is an alumna of the Kenya School of Government’s Strategic Leadership Development Programme and writes on county public service reform, wage bill management, and the cooperative sector. title: Financial discipline: The missing key to Kenya’s youth prosperity
description: Young Kenyans are earning more than ever — but without financial discipline, income alone will not build the secure future they deserve. By Flora Jebet Financial discipline among Kenya’s young people has never mattered more. With the cost of living rising and economic competition intensifying, the gap between earning money and managing it effectively is widening — and it is costing a generation its financial future. Across the country, young people are generating income through employment, entrepreneurship, online businesses, and the informal sector. Yet earning is only half the equation. Social media, peer pressure, and lifestyle aspirations are driving uncontrolled spending on clothing, entertainment, and outings that consume income before it can work. Without a budget, there is no framework to distinguish needs from wants — and money that could build a future is spent on things that offer none. The solution begins with fundamentals. Every amount received should have a purpose: basic needs, bills, family obligations, savings, or investment. A simple written budget transforms vague intentions into accountable decisions. Saving need not wait for a larger salary — consistent small amounts, set aside as a habit, compound into meaningful security over time and reduce reliance on the high-interest digital loans that now trap many young borrowers. Financial literacy must also be treated as essential education. Schools, universities, families, and community organisations all carry responsibility for equipping young people with the tools to budget, manage debt, and invest intelligently. Financial independence is not built in a single pay cheque. It is built in the daily decisions that most people never see. title: Wenger considers shock bid for FIFA presidency
description: The former Arsenal manager is weighing a challenge to Gianni Infantino ahead of the November 18 candidate deadline for the March 2027 election. By Pascal Okoth Arsène Wenger is seriously considering entering the race for the FIFA presidency, with reports from The Athletic, BBC Sport and other international outlets indicating the 75-year-old Frenchman may declare his candidacy before the November 18 deadline. The election is scheduled for 18 March 2027, during the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco. Wenger would challenge incumbent Gianni Infantino, the Swiss-Italian administrator who has held the presidency since 2016 and is seeking a fourth term after re-elections in 2019 and 2023. No official declaration has been made, but influential figures within European football are actively encouraging Wenger to stand — UEFA among them, though the governing body is simultaneously evaluating other potential candidates. The push for an alternative reflects growing unease with Infantino’s leadership, particularly following a controversial proposal to allow private investors to acquire a minority stake in a company tied to FIFA’s commercial operations and World Cup activities. The plan drew sharp criticism from UEFA and several confederations before Infantino withdrew it. Wenger publicly distanced himself from the project, stating he had no involvement in its development and supporting its withdrawal. His FIFA credentials are substantial. Since joining the organisation in November 2019 as Chief of Global Football Development, Wenger has driven youth development initiatives, coaching education programmes, and the establishment of football academies across multiple continents — giving him an operational understanding of FIFA’s structures that few outside candidates could claim. The obstacles, however, are real. Infantino retains significant support among FIFA’s 211 member associations, particularly across Africa, Asia, and South America — the voting blocs that have historically determined presidential outcomes. Any candidate must also secure nominations from at least five member associations to qualify, a threshold that requires early diplomatic groundwork. Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima and former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega have also been named as potential challengers. Questions about Wenger’s age have surfaced — at 77, some observers have questioned whether he would commit to a full four-year term. Those close to him reportedly believe his experience and institutional knowledge outweigh that concern. The football world has not seen a credible challenge to a sitting FIFA president in years. If Wenger declares, that changes immediately. His 22-year tenure at Arsenal — three Premier League titles, seven FA Cups, and a redefinition of English football’s tactical and cultural possibilities — gave him global standing that no other candidate in this race can match. Whether that translates into the kind of association-by-association political support needed to unseat Infantino is the question his camp must now answer. The November 18 deadline is days away. What Wenger decides in that window could define not just his next chapter, but the direction of world football for years to come. title: UDA questions Gachagua’s status as DCP leader
description: The ruling party claims the former Deputy President is not formally recognised as party leader in Registrar of Political Parties records, adding to tensions ahead of 2027. By Yvonne Wambui The United Democratic Alliance yesterday questioned Rigathi Gachagua’s position as leader of the Democracy for the Citizens Party, claiming he is not officially listed in records held by the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties. According to information attributed to the Registrar, the position of party leader is not among the offices currently registered under DCP. The records instead identify former Kakamega Senator Cleophas Malala as the party’s registered Deputy Party Leader. The claim has reignited debate over the leadership and registration status of Gachagua’s party, raising questions about whether the procedures required to formalise his appointment were completed. Under the Political Parties Act, any changes to registered party officials must be submitted to the Registrar through the prescribed legal process — a requirement that applies regardless of how a party presents its leadership structure internally or publicly. Gachagua launched DCP in May 2025 following his fallout with UDA and has since presented himself publicly as the party’s leader, using it to mobilise supporters and build a national political network ahead of the 2027 General Election. He has worked to attract politicians, community leaders, and regional networks to the party as he consolidates his standing as one of the most prominent opposition voices in the country. UDA’s challenge introduces a fresh complication to that project — specifically the legal distinction between internal party appointments and offices formally recognised by the Registrar. Whether Gachagua’s leadership carries standing under registration law is now a live question, and one that his party will need to address directly if it is to avoid the issue being used as sustained political ammunition. The development comes against a backdrop of deepening tensions between Gachagua and the current administration, with both sides increasingly active in positioning ahead of the August 2027 poll. With the election drawing closer, the dispute over DCP’s registration status is unlikely to fade quietly. The post UDA questions Gachagua’s status as DCP leader appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.
