title: Waiguru leads Kindiki in running mate poll as Ruto’s 2027 ticket takes shape
description: A Swiss Poll International survey has placed Kirinyaga Governor Anne Waiguru ahead of Deputy President Kithure Kindiki as the preferred running mate for President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election, in findings that are already reshaping the conversation about Kenya’s next electoral contest. By Daniel Karanja Kirinyaga Governor Anne Waiguru has emerged as the leading preferred running mate for President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election, commanding 42 per cent support in a Swiss Poll International survey that places her ahead of Deputy President Kithure Kindiki at 31 per cent and Homa Bay Governor Gladys Wanga at 13 per cent — findings that land at a moment when Kenya’s pre-election political calculations are intensifying by the week. The poll, conducted nationally, offers the clearest public snapshot yet of how Kenyans are thinking about the question of who should stand beside Ruto on the 2027 ticket — and its results carry implications that extend well beyond a simple popularity ranking. They touch on regional arithmetic, gender politics, the future of the Deputy President’s position, and the broader strategic question of what kind of coalition Ruto needs to build if he is to retain the presidency in what is shaping up to be the most competitive Kenyan election in a generation. Waiguru’s 42 per cent showing is striking for several reasons. She is a two-term governor of Kirinyaga County, a former Cabinet Secretary for Devolution and Planning under President Uhuru Kenyatta, and one of the most recognisable political figures in the Mount Kenya region — a vote-rich bloc whose support will be fiercely contested in 2027. Her profile combines executive experience at both national and county level with a political resilience that has seen her survive an impeachment attempt, a series of legal battles and the shifting loyalties of a region whose political direction has rarely been more uncertain. For Ruto, whose relationship with the Mount Kenya establishment has been complicated by the fallout with Kenyatta and the subsequent realignment of figures such as former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, the idea of a running mate who can anchor the region carries obvious strategic appeal. Kindiki, at 31 per cent, occupies a fundamentally different position in this calculation. As the sitting Deputy President, he is not merely a potential running mate — he is already on the ticket, elevated to the position following Gachagua’s controversial impeachment in late 2024. His poll numbers reflect a figure who has had relatively little time to establish an independent public profile in the role, having spent much of his tenure navigating the institutional aftermath of his predecessor’s removal while managing a demanding security portfolio. His academic background — he is a distinguished constitutional law scholar and former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Nairobi — commands respect, but respect and electoral warmth are different currencies, and the poll suggests Waiguru currently holds more of the latter. Wanga’s 13 per cent is the most politically nuanced figure in the survey. As governor of Homa Bay County, she represents a constituency that sits at the heart of ODM’s traditional support base in Luo Nyanza. Her appearance in a poll about Ruto’s preferred running mate reflects two possibilities that are not mutually exclusive: genuine cross-community admiration for her governance record, and the complex negotiations between Kenya Kwanza and ODM that have characterised the broad-based government arrangement. Whether Wanga’s figure represents a serious political pathway or simply a measure of her personal popularity is a question the coming months will begin to answer. The deeper significance of this poll lies in what it reveals about the structural pressures bearing down on Ruto’s 2027 campaign. The President faces a fundamentally different electoral environment from the one he navigated in 2022. Then, he ran as an insurgent — the hustler candidate challenging the establishment, drawing energy from economic frustration and a generational desire for change. That narrative delivered him the presidency by a margin that was ultimately confirmed by the Supreme Court after a legal challenge. In 2027, he runs as an incumbent with a record to defend, in an economy that has tested ordinary Kenyans severely through the cost-of-living pressures that dominated the 2024 protest movement, and against an opposition that is — however imperfectly — moving towards the kind of unity that eluded it last time. In that context, the choice of running mate is not a ceremonial decision. It is a strategic one that will signal to specific communities, regions and demographic groups whether Ruto’s coalition is broadening or contracting. Waiguru’s strength in the poll suggests that a significant portion of Kenyans see value in a ticket that doubles down on Mount Kenya representation — a reading that prioritises consolidating a base over reaching for new constituencies. Kindiki’s position, by contrast, represents continuity and institutional stability, virtues that carry weight in uncertain times but that may not generate the electoral excitement a competitive race demands. What the poll cannot capture is the internal negotiation that will ultimately determine the ticket. Kenyan running mate selections are rarely decided by public preference surveys alone. They are the product of backroom conversations between regional barons, party structures, financial interests and the kind of political debts that accumulate over years of alliance-building. Waiguru’s public numbers are strong, but public numbers and private commitments are different things. What is clear is that the 2027 ticket question is now firmly open and firmly contested. Gachagua’s departure from the Deputy President’s office removed what many assumed was a settled arrangement and introduced a fluidity into Ruto’s re-election planning that his campaign strategists will be working hard to manage. Every poll that places Waiguru ahead of Kindiki adds pressure to that management exercise and raises questions — however premature — about whether the sitting Deputy President’s position on the ticket is as secure as the institution of his office might suggest. Kenya’s election season has, in effect, already begun. title: Gachagua warns Ruto to respect Kenyatta: ‘In nine months you will also be a former president’
description: The former Deputy President has issued his sharpest personal warning yet to Ruto, framing the treatment of Kenyatta as a measure of the man — and a preview of his own fate. By David Kimani Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has warned President William Ruto to treat retired President Uhuru Kenyatta with respect, telling him directly that in nine months he too will be a former president and that the courtesy he withholds today will be the courtesy he cannot claim tomorrow. Gachagua made the remarks in a video circulated widely on social media, delivering what has become his most pointed personal challenge to Ruto since his impeachment from the deputy presidency. “Respect the former president,” he said. “In nine months’ time you will also be a former. Respect is mutual.” The statement was brief, deliberate and calculated — the kind of message designed not merely to be heard but to land. The warning comes at a moment of intensifying pre-election tension, with opposition leaders coalescing around the shared position that Ruto’s administration has treated Kenyatta with a contempt unbefitting of a former Head of State. Gachagua, who now positions himself as a central figure in the emerging opposition architecture, has repeatedly invoked Kenyatta’s treatment as evidence of the administration’s character. The subtext of his message is as important as the words themselves. With August 2027 drawing closer, Gachagua is telling Ruto — and telling Kenya — that power is temporary, accountability is not, and that the clock is already running. title: Gachagua breaks silence on Ruto’s attacks: ‘I was mourning — now I have buried my sister’
description: The DCP leader has warned President Ruto that his period of restraint is over, challenging Kenya’s Catholic bishops to confront the President directly over language he says is beneath the dignity of the office. By Grace Wanja Democracy for the Citizens Party leader Rigathi Gachagua yesterday broke his silence over President William Ruto’s recent personal attacks, revealing that he had held back only because he was mourning the death of his sister — and warning that now she has been buried, any further insults from the President will be met with an immediate and full response. Gachagua made the remarks during a church service on Sunday, one day after burying his sister, in what turned out to be one of his most carefully framed public addresses since his impeachment from the Deputy Presidency. The timing and setting were deliberate. By speaking from a church, fresh from grief, he positioned himself not as a combative politician spoiling for a fight but as a man who had shown restraint under provocation and was now simply and reasonably serving notice that the restraint had run its course. His target was specific. Ruto had used a tour of Kisii County to describe Gachagua as a “master of hate,” a “hate man from Texas,” a “chronic liar,” a “conman” and a “fraud” — a sequence of personal attacks delivered from public platforms during official county engagements that drew criticism from several quarters, including the Catholic Church. Gachagua’s response on Sunday was measured in tone but unambiguous in substance. “This week you have been in Kisii, insulting Rigathi Gachagua and Uhuru Kenyatta. You were lucky I was mourning and did not get an opportunity to respond to you,” he said. “But now that I have buried my sister, if you insult us this week, we will respond.” The statement carried a weight that went beyond political point-scoring. Gachagua was making two arguments simultaneously — one personal, one institutional. The personal argument was that he had shown the kind of human dignity in a moment of family grief that he believes his former principal has failed to demonstrate in public office. The institutional argument was more pointed: that the President of Kenya has a responsibility to protect the dignity of the office he holds, not merely for his own sake but for the sake of everyone who aspires to hold it in the future. “He is undermining the dignity and the respect of the institution of the presidency,” Gachagua said. “We want to become presidents of Kenya, and we do not want the respect of the office of the President to go down.” It was a line that served double duty — a criticism of Ruto’s conduct and a quiet declaration of his own ambitions, framed as concern for the institution rather than personal grievance. The Catholic Church had entered the fray days earlier. The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops, led by chairman Archbishop Maurice Muhatia, issued a statement on Thursday calling on presidential aspirants to avoid tribal, hateful and demeaning language as political exchanges intensified ahead of August 2027. The bishops’ appeal was directed broadly, but its timing — following Ruto’s Kisii remarks — left little doubt about the context in which it was issued. Gachagua welcomed the intervention but redirected it with considerable precision. “I have seen Catholic bishops saying leaders should not use abusive language against each other. And that is right. But let me help them a little. It is not the other leaders who are using abusive language. The person using insults everywhere is the President of the Republic of Kenya,” he said. He then went further, issuing a direct challenge to the bishops to request a formal meeting with Ruto and address his conduct face to face. “We want to tell our Catholic fathers that they are right, but they should get an appointment with William Ruto, with our church leaders, go and sit him down and tell him what he is doing is not presidential,” he stated. He extended the appeal beyond the Catholic Church, calling on bishops of the African Inland Church, the Anglican Church of Kenya and the Presbyterian Church of East Africa to intervene. His appeal to the AIC was particularly pointed, given that Ruto is a worshipping member of that church. “First, AIC, you are the bishops who should go and sit down with him. Tell him that he has embarrassed the church because of the insults coming from his mouth while he is the President of the Republic of Kenya,” Gachagua said. The broader political context in which these exchanges are taking place matters enormously. Kenya is now less than a year from a General Election that is shaping up to be fiercely contested across every level of government. The opposition, however imperfectly, is consolidating — with Gachagua, Kalonzo Musyoka, Martha Karua, Ndindi Nyoro and others moving, however gradually, towards a common platform. Ruto, as the incumbent, faces the challenge of defending a record on the economy and governance that has drawn sustained criticism, while simultaneously managing the internal dynamics of a ruling coalition that has itself been tested by the Gachagua impeachment and its aftermath. In that environment, the register of political speech matters. When a sitting president calls a former deputy president a conman and a fraud from public platforms in a county that he is visiting on what are ostensibly official duties, it sets a tone for political discourse that filters down through every level of public life. When that former deputy president responds from a church, a day after burying his sister, by challenging religious leaders to hold the President to account, the exchange has moved well beyond a personal quarrel. Gachagua left one door open. “If he stops, we will return to policies,” he said. “If he gets into insults, we will meet him there. He is the one to set the agenda because he is the President.” The agenda, for now, appears firmly set. title: Kalonzo links Ruto to cement firms as building collapses mount, demands KSh 204B Safaricom return
description: The Wiper leader used a church pulpit in Mwingi to launch his sharpest attack yet on the Ruto administration, connecting political corruption to deadly construction failures and an unconstitutional share sale. By Daniel Karanja Wiper Patriotic Front Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka yesterday accused President William Ruto’s administration of allowing politically connected individuals to profit from Kenya’s cement industry, linking what he described as systemic corruption to a string of deadly building collapses that have claimed lives across the country in recent weeks. Kalonzo made the allegations during a worship service at Word of Faith Church in Mwingi Central on Sunday, delivering remarks that combined religious conviction with some of the most direct political accusations he has levelled against Ruto since the two emerged as adversaries ahead of the 2027 General Election. The choice of a church setting — before a congregation he described as “the salt of the earth” — was deliberate, casting his political challenge in moral as well as institutional terms. “For every single bag of cement, there is a percentage going to Mr Ruto,” Kalonzo alleged, making a claim he did not substantiate with documentary evidence but that he framed as the logical explanation for the proliferation of substandard construction materials in the market. He argued that politically connected interests had penetrated the supply chains for essential building materials, compromising quality standards and leaving ordinary Kenyans to bear the lethal consequences. His remarks came against the backdrop of renewed and urgent public concern about building safety in Nairobi and its surrounding areas, following multiple structural collapses that have drawn attention to the quality of construction materials, the enforcement of building codes and the capacity of regulatory authorities to hold contractors and developers to account. “Imagine how many people have died this month because one building collapses, then another collapses. Syokimau,” Kalonzo said, invoking a specific location as shorthand for a pattern of disaster that he argued was neither accidental nor inevitable. “It is impunity and the presence of cement companies producing poor quality. When a building is constructed with this, it collapses,” he added, calling for the government to act decisively against manufacturers whose products he claimed were failing to meet basic safety standards. The government has not publicly responded to Kalonzo’s specific allegations about cement industry interests. The building safety crisis, if it can be called that, is real regardless of its political framing. Construction-related fatalities in Kenya have been a recurring and tragic feature of urban growth, driven by a combination of rapidly expanding demand for affordable housing, inconsistent enforcement of building regulations, the widespread use of unverified construction materials and a culture of impunity among developers who cut corners on specifications. When a prominent political leader stands before a congregation and connects those deaths to corruption at the highest level of government, the accusation lands with emotional force that official denials struggle to match. Kalonzo used the same platform to describe the Ruto administration as a “predator regime” — language that marked a significant escalation in his public characterisation of the government and signalled his intent to run a campaign built as much on moral condemnation as on policy contrast. “This is why I’m saying heavy lifting. Heavy lifting to get rid of this predator regime,” he declared, casting the 2027 election not as a routine democratic contest but as a civic emergency requiring extraordinary collective effort. He positioned himself explicitly as a constitutional lawyer committed to the rule of law, pointing to his personal participation in court proceedings as evidence of that commitment. “I am a constitutional lawyer. And that is who I am. You can even see that I go to court myself to defend it,” he said, drawing a contrast with what he portrayed as an administration willing to override legal and institutional constraints for political and financial advantage. That contrast found its sharpest expression in Kalonzo’s remarks about the KSh 204B Safaricom transaction, which he raised directly with the congregation. He was referring to the government’s sale of a 15 per cent stake in Safaricom to Vodacom, a transaction that generated approximately KSh 204.3B in proceeds, with a further KSh 40.2B paid upfront in exchange for future dividends on the government’s remaining stake — combined proceeds of KSh 244.5B that were channelled into the National Infrastructure Fund. The High Court has since declared the divestiture unconstitutional, null and void, ruling that it was undertaken without adequate public participation and ordering the shares transferred to Vodacom to be restored to the government on behalf of Kenyans. The ruling has raised complex and unresolved questions about the fate of money already received, the mechanics of share restoration and the accountability of those who authorised the transaction. “He is supposed to have returned 204 billion shillings. That is a lot of money,” Kalonzo told the congregation, framing the sum not as an abstract financial figure but as a measure of what ordinary Kenyans had been denied. The cumulative effect of Kalonzo’s Mwingi address was a portrait of an administration he characterises as predatory, corrupt and constitutionally reckless — one that profits from cement bags, presides over collapsing buildings and sells national assets without public consent. Whether those characterisations are legally sustainable or politically persuasive to a broad electorate is a question the coming months will test. What is beyond doubt is that Kalonzo is running, that he is running hard and that he has chosen to frame his campaign around accountability, constitutionalism and the daily economic suffering of ordinary Kenyans. With August 2027 less than a year away, the congregation in Mwingi was not merely a church service. It was a campaign opening, delivered from a pulpit, aimed at a nation the Wiper leader believes is ready for what he called the heavy lifting of change. title: Notorious motorbike-riding thugs arrested by patrol cops after a dramatic chase - Suspected stolen mobile phones seized (PHOTO)
description: Monday, November 16, 2026 - Police officers have arrested three suspected phone snatchers following a dramatic chase along Kangundo Road in Nairobi's East Sub-Region, leading to the recovery of eight mobile phones and other items believed to be linked to criminal activities. According to the National Police Service (NPS), officers on patrol near Obama Police Station spotted a suspicious motorcycle carrying two pillion passengers, both wearing balaclavas. When the officers moved to intercept them, one of the passengers jumped off the motorcycle while the rider sped off towards Saika with the other passenger. The officers gave chase and managed to apprehend the passenger who had alighted. Acting on leads obtained from him, they proceeded to Mowlem, where they recovered the motorcycle and arrested its rider. third suspect, who had initially escaped, was subsequently traced and arrested at a makeshift single-room dwelling. A search of the premises led to the recovery of eight assorted mobile phones, a knife, an imitation firearm incapable of firing, and government stores. three suspects were escorted to Obama Police Station, where they were placed in custody as investigations continue. recovered items have been secured as exhibits. National Police Service says it will continue conducting patrols and pursuing leads to disrupt criminal activities, recover stolen property and apprehend suspects. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Melco Kenya Faces Questions Over Medical Equipment Imports as Jayesh Saini's Name Resurfaces in Controversial Spyware Case
description: Questions have emerged over the customs clearance of three consignments of medical imaging equipment imported by Melco (K) Ltd, following claims that invoices submitted during the clearance process carried substantially lower values than those originally associated with the shipments. The controversy has placed the company and its director, Prakash Saini brother to Jayesh Saini, under scrutiny over the declared value of the equipment and the amount of government levies paid during importation. This publication sought clarification on the valuation of the equipment, customs declarations, applicable levies and the reported detention of three containers. Shipping documents reviewed by the publication indicated that each of the three consignments was initially supported by a pro forma invoice valued at US$5,337,147.12. That places the combined initial pro forma value of the three consignments at approximately US$16.01 million. The central question is why invoices reflecting substantially lower amounts were said to have been presented during customs clearance and whether those changes affected the Railway Development Levy and Import Declaration Fee payable to the Kenya Revenue Authority. The distinction is important because customs declarations must comply with applicable valuation rules. An invoice discrepancy does not automatically establish tax evasion, but a substantial unexplained reduction in declared value warrants examination, particularly where millions of dollars in imported medical equipment are involved. The publication asked Melco to explain who authorised the alleged invoice revisions, whether the company declared the correct customs values and how much it paid in RDL and IDF. According to the publication, no substantive response was received by the requested deadline of noon on July 31, 2026. The company has not been shown to have admitted any wrongdoing, and the original supplier invoices, final customs declarations and payment records have not been independently verified for this article. The investigation also identified three containers linked to the consignments: MRSU3665310/ML-CN4816132, CSGU6476654/CU008234 and PIDU4279792/CX0550787. The questionnaire stated that the containers were reportedly being held at Autoports Container Freight Stations in Nairobi and Mombasa. Melco was asked to explain the reasons for the reported holds, whether the Kenya Revenue Authority or another government agency was investigating the shipments, and whether the company had received formal notification of any irregularities. The current status of the containers remains unconfirmed. Another issue concerns a VAT exemption that the questionnaire says Melco obtained from the Ministry of Health through a letter dated June 12, 2026. The publication expressly stated that it was not questioning the VAT exemption itself. Instead, it sought to establish whether that exemption had any bearing on the valuation used to calculate RDL and IDF. These are separate issues that require examination of the applicable tax provisions and the specific exemption documents. The controversy comes against the backdrop of a separate, widely reported legal dispute involving businessman Jayesh Saini, whose name has appeared in court proceedings concerning a proposed digital communications and surveillance platform. In a lawsuit filed by software developer Mary Wachuka Maina and her company Jipe Inc., Saini was named alongside senior government figures, including Head of Public Service Felix Koskei, former Treasury Principal Secretary Chris Kiptoo and President William Ruto's speechwriter Eric Ng'eno. According to court documents reported by the Daily Nation and The Standard, the developer claimed that the proposed software would have been capable of monitoring critics, managing political messaging and countering negative commentary about the government. Wachuka further claimed that Saini was introduced as a person expected to oversee aspects of the proposed project's financing and implementation. Saini denied involvement in the alleged scheme, describing the claims against him as baseless. Other defendants also disputed the allegations, including the suggestion that government officials had authorised an unlawful surveillance project. The proposed arrangement eventually became the subject of a multimillion-shilling commercial dispute. In June 2026, the High Court dismissed applications by several defendants, including Saini, seeking to be removed from the proceedings. The court found that the dispute raised issues requiring examination at trial. That procedural ruling did not establish that the alleged surveillance project had been authorised, that Saini financed it or that any defendant committed wrongdoing. The spyware litigation and the Melco import questions are distinct matters. No evidence reviewed for this article establishes that the two transactions were connected. Nevertheless, both controversies underline the importance of transparency where private commercial interests intersect with public institutions and government decision-making. In the Melco matter, the most pressing questions remain straightforward. What was the actual transaction value of each medical equipment consignment? Why were lower invoice values reportedly presented during clearance? What customs valuation method was applied? How much was paid in government levies? And what explains the reported detention of the containers? These are questions that can be resolved through the production of commercial invoices, customs entry records, exemption documents and official payment receipts. The Kenya Revenue Authority is also in a position to establish whether the declarations complied with customs law, subject to the confidentiality requirements governing taxpayer information. For a company importing high-value medical equipment into Kenya, providing a clear explanation would help address concerns about compliance and protect public confidence in the integrity of the importation process. Until the relevant records are examined, the allegations of undervaluation remain unresolved. The public interest, however, is substantial. Kenya's healthcare sector depends on medical equipment supplied through both public and private institutions, and the proper declaration of imported goods is essential to maintaining accountability in the country's revenue system. The unanswered questions are sufficiently serious to warrant a transparent, documented explanation.

author: xinhua media
title: Music bridges cultures, deepens friendship at Chinese concert in Kenya
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia A Chinese concert featuring traditional folk music and cross-cultural performances was held in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, on Saturday evening, offering audiences a 70-minute musical showcase celebrating China-Africa friendship. NAIROBI, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) — A Chinese concert featuring traditional folk music and cross-cultural performances was held in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, on Saturday evening, offering audiences a 70-minute musical showcase celebrating China-Africa friendship. Titled “Golden Bell Resounds, Harmony Along the Silk Road,” the concert, organized by the Beijing Federation of Literary and Art Circles and undertaken by China Arts and Entertainment Group Ltd., brought together Chinese and African artists at the Kenya National Theater. The performance featured a diverse repertoire, including popular Chinese classics and arrangements blending traditional Chinese folk music with classical piano. “It is my great honor to come to Kenya this time and introduce Chinese culture to local audiences,” said renowned Chinese singer Wu Bixia, who performed the Yunnan folk song “The River Flows Clear.” Ma Xinming, executive vice chairman of the Beijing Federation of Literary and Art Circles, said this African tour aims to honor the consensus of the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges. “With music, it creates a platform for heart-to-heart dialogue, promotes cultural exchanges, deepens mutual understanding between the Chinese and Kenyan peoples and consolidates the people-to-people foundation of China-Africa friendship,” he said. The concert concluded with a joint performance of “Jambo Bwana,” a popular welcome song across East Africa. As the artists played, audience members hummed along, followed by sustained applause at the end of the performance. Ma said the troupe would continue its African tour in Ethiopia after the Kenya performance, expressing hope that the artists would visit more African countries in the future to further promote cultural exchanges and share stories of China-Africa friendship. ■ The post Music bridges cultures, deepens friendship at Chinese concert in Kenya appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: TSC teacher termly classroom lesson observation: Why it matters for Kenya’s schools
description: The Teachers Service Commission’s structured lesson observation framework is transforming classroom accountability and professional growth across Kenya’s public schools. By Ashford Kimani The Teachers Service Commission’s termly classroom lesson observation is one of the most consequential tools shaping the quality of teaching in Kenya’s public schools today — and yet it remains widely misunderstood. Required at least once every term, the observation forms a core component of every teacher’s online termly appraisal and focuses on three interconnected areas: content delivery, teaching techniques, and learner involvement. Far from being a bureaucratic box-ticking exercise, it is a carefully structured mechanism for raising standards, ensuring accountability, and driving professional growth in classrooms across the country. Structured lesson observation brings clarity and consistency to the evaluation of teaching in an environment where perceptions of good practice can easily become subjective. Without a common framework, one observer might prioritise content mastery, another classroom management, and a third learner engagement — with each arriving at entirely different conclusions about the same lesson. The TSC’s standardised observation form addresses this directly by establishing shared, transparent expectations of what effective teaching looks like. It levels the playing field across subjects, grade levels, and school environments, ensuring that learners — regardless of which teacher stands at the front of their classroom — receive a minimum standard of quality instruction. In this respect, lesson observation is as much about equity as it is about accountability. The accountability dimension is real and important. Teaching, like medicine or law, demands adherence to professional standards. When teachers know their practice may be observed and evaluated against clear criteria, they are more likely to plan thoroughly, use their time purposefully, and remain focused on what learners actually take away from a lesson. This is not surveillance — it is professional discipline of the kind that any high-performing field expects of its practitioners. The observation framework discourages complacency and reinforces the principle that what happens inside a classroom must be intentional, evidence-based, and aligned with curriculum goals. Where the TSC framework truly distinguishes itself, however, is in its capacity to generate meaningful professional development. Vague feedback — “improve your teaching methods” — helps no one. The structured observation form makes it possible for an observer to point to specific, verifiable indicators: the range of instructional strategies deployed, the degree of learner participation, the quality of questioning, or the effectiveness with which a lesson was concluded. That level of specificity transforms feedback from a verdict into a roadmap. For early-career teachers still finding their footing, this kind of targeted guidance is invaluable. For experienced educators, it offers a structured prompt for honest self-reflection and prevents the kind of professional stagnation that can quietly take hold even in capable classrooms. The framework’s emphasis on learner involvement reflects a wider shift in educational thinking that Kenya has increasingly embraced. For decades, the dominant model prioritised content coverage — getting through the syllabus — with comparatively little attention paid to how learners actually engaged with the material. The competency-based curriculum has challenged that orthodoxy, placing active learning, critical thinking, and skill development at the heart of classroom practice. The TSC’s observation tool reinforces this shift by explicitly assessing learner participation, interaction, and questioning. It pushes teachers to move away from passive instruction and towards environments where learners are genuinely involved in constructing their own understanding. The result, when implemented well, is classrooms that produce not just students who can recall information, but young people who can think, communicate, and collaborate. For school leaders — Heads of Department, Deans of Studies, and Deputies — the observation process provides something that no end-of-term report or examination result can fully offer: firsthand, real-time insight into what is actually happening in classrooms. It allows leaders to identify recurring weaknesses in content delivery, spot underuse of teaching resources, and design targeted interventions grounded in evidence rather than assumption. When patterns emerge across multiple observations — whether in a single department or across the whole school — they become a basis for institutional improvement: informing decisions about professional development, resource allocation, and curriculum support in ways that genuinely move the needle. It is fair to acknowledge that no tool is without limitations. Critics of structured observation forms often point to binary or checklist-style scoring systems as overly reductive, unable to capture the full complexity and artistry of skilled teaching. The concern is not without merit. A numerical score, taken in isolation, cannot reflect the relationship a teacher has built with a class over a term, the differentiation happening beneath the surface of a lesson, or the quiet breakthrough a struggling learner had that afternoon. But this is an argument for enriching the process — combining scores with detailed qualitative commentary and genuine professional dialogue — not for abandoning the framework altogether. Used thoughtfully, the two approaches are complementary, not competing. Ultimately, the value of the TSC classroom lesson observation depends not on the form itself but on the culture in which it operates. When it is approached as a punitive measure — something to be endured and survived — it produces anxiety, defensiveness, and performances rather than genuine teaching. When it is treated as a professional conversation, rooted in evidence and oriented towards growth, it becomes one of the most powerful levers available for improving the quality of education. Kenya’s teachers deserve a system that takes their professional development seriously. The TSC’s termly observation framework, implemented with honesty, consistency, and genuine commitment to improvement, is a credible foundation for exactly that. title: Five hustles that can grow KSh 10,000 to KSh 100,000 in 30 days in Nairobi
description: From mitumba trading to freelancing, Nairobi’s streets and digital platforms are offering young entrepreneurs a credible shot at rapid returns on modest capital. By Yvonne Wambui Five small businesses available to Nairobi entrepreneurs with as little as KSh 10,000 have been identified as holding genuine potential to grow that capital tenfold within 30 days — provided they are managed with discipline, strategy and consistent reinvestment. As the cost of living rises and formal employment remains out of reach for many young Kenyans, side hustles and small enterprises have moved from fallback option to primary income source for a growing number of people. The five opportunities outlined here span physical trade, food vending, digital commerce and skills-based work — meaning there is a viable entry point regardless of background or prior experience. Mitumba selling tops the list and remains one of the most accessible businesses in the city. Traders source second-hand clothing from markets such as Gikomba and River Road at low wholesale prices and resell at a margin through physical stalls or, increasingly, via WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram. The shift to social media has removed the barrier of shop rental, allowing sellers to reach customers across Nairobi and beyond from a smartphone. Street food vending is the second opportunity and one of the most immediately profitable for those willing to put in the hours. Selling smokies, boiled eggs and affordable snacks at bus stops, construction sites, universities and busy office areas requires minimal capital and can generate consistent daily income. The formula is straightforward: good hygiene, competitive pricing and a high-footfall location. Get those three right and a street food business can scale quickly. Fresh juice and fruit vending is the third hustle and a natural fit for Nairobi’s urban pace. Entrepreneurs buy watermelons, mangoes and pineapples in bulk from wholesale markets and convert them into fresh juice or ready-to-eat portions for commuters and office workers seeking affordable refreshments. Demand is strong, margins are reasonable and the business can be operated from a single cart or table. Freelancing is the fourth option and the most skills-dependent on the list. Young people with abilities in writing, graphic design, social media management or virtual assistance can market their services through LinkedIn, Twitter and local Facebook groups to build a client base without any physical stock or premises. The barrier to entry is internet access and the confidence to pitch — both increasingly within reach for Nairobi’s youth. Online selling through dropshipping and social commerce rounds out the five. This model allows entrepreneurs to market clothing, shoes, beauty products and household accessories through WhatsApp Business and Facebook without holding significant inventory, arranging delivery only once a sale is confirmed. It is lean, low-risk and scalable. A word of honest caution: turning KSh 10,000 into KSh 100,000 in a single month is not guaranteed and requires genuine commitment, smart reinvestment and an understanding of customers’ needs. Those operating physical businesses must also comply with Nairobi County licensing requirements, and food handlers are expected to meet public health standards. Success in any of these ventures is determined not by the size of the starting capital, but by the quality of the decisions made with it. title: Forgery Season in Kenya: Disputed Wills, Missing Shares and Claims of Witness Intimidation Rock High-Profile Court Battles
description: From disputed wills and allegedly forged share transfers to accusations of witness intimidation and manipulation of police investigations, Kenya appears to be confronting an epidemic of questionable documents, judicial manoeuvres and extraordinary impunity. It must be forgery season in Kenya. Not the kind announced by the Meteorological Department, but one characterised by suspicious signatures, disputed wills, questionable share transfers and seemingly endless litigation. One might be forgiven for wondering whether forgery has become an occupational hazard of wealth, inheritance and corporate ownership. When substantial estates are involved, the dead cannot speak, documents mysteriously emerge, and those challenging their authenticity find themselves fighting exhausting legal battles. Consider the ongoing murder proceedings involving Dutch businessman Tob Cohen. Forensic testimony has raised serious questions about signatures on documents attributed to the deceased, including his disputed Will. The allegations surrounding Sarah Wairimu Cohen's case demonstrate how even the final wishes of the dead can become entangled in controversies over document authenticity. Whether the documents are ultimately declared forged remains a matter for judicial determination. Then there is the estate of the late Dr. James Boro Karugu, Kenya's second Attorney General, whose distinguished legacy of public service, law and business has become overshadowed by a bitter succession dispute involving a purported Will and Settlement Trust Deed. Investigations by the Directorate of Criminal Investigations have raised serious allegations concerning the authenticity of these documents, with proposed criminal charges reportedly approved by the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. At the centre of this controversy stands Peter Gachuhi of Kaplan & Stratton, whose association with the disputed testamentary documents and the administration of the estate has attracted intense scrutiny. Despite the gravity of the allegations, Gachuhi has pursued constitutional proceedings challenging his intended prosecution. These proceedings have for now had the intended effect of temporarily frustrating accountability. And how many legal applications must be exhausted before justice can take its course? The number is finite, even as Peter Gachuhi laughs at James Karugu’s grave after having escaped arrest. The controversy becomes even more extraordinary when one examines a separate criminal case involving the queen of forgery, Jane Kabiu of Optimum Registrar’s, Eric Mwaura Karugu and their partner Brenda Irungu, a hostile witness whom they have been tampering with . In Republic v Eric Mwaura Karugu, Jane Wangechi Kabiu and Benjamin Githara Karugu , Criminal Case No. E644 of 2025, the accused face charges arising from the alleged fraudulent transfer of a share belonging to Victoria Nyambura Karugu from Mathara Holdings Limited to Centurion Holdings Limited. The charges include conspiracy to defraud, forgery, uttering a false document and giving false information to a public officer, with different counts applying to the respective accused. With nothing short of blatant arrogance, the accused persons sought to reduce their cash bail from KES 700,000 each to a mere KES 20,000, or alternatively obtain personal bond, arguing that the disputed share had a nominal value of KES 100. What extraordinary reasoning! Since when did the face value of a share determine the seriousness of an alleged forgery? Does a falsified document become less criminal because it bears a small monetary figure? The issue is not simply the nominal value of a share but the alleged manipulation of corporate ownership records and the violation of proprietary rights. They must have thought the Court was retarded. Fortunately, on 21 October 2026, Principal Magistrate Hon. Carolyne Nyaguthii Mugo was not persuaded. In a carefully reasoned ruling, she dismissed the application, maintaining the existing KES 700,000 cash bail and accompanying conditions. The magistrate recognised the constitutional presumption of innocence and the requirement that bail remain reasonable, but concluded that the applicants had not demonstrated sufficient grounds for the substantial reduction sought. What makes the application particularly astonishing is the conduct alleged by the prosecution during the proceedings. The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions raised concerns about witness interference involving Brenda Wanjiru Irungu, a former Mathara Holdings employee, and disputed Board resolutions allegedly connected to attempts to influence her. The prosecution also referred to the accused persons' alleged failure to attend scheduled court proceedings, notwithstanding their assurances of compliance with bail conditions. More troubling were allegations concerning interference with police investigations. A complaint against OCS John Marubu of Kanunga Police Station was investigated by the National Police Service Internal Affairs Unit. In a letter dated 16 July 2026, Internal Affairs confirmed that the Inspector General had concurred with its recommendations and directed disciplinary action against the officer. Then came allegations of an incident bordering on the unimaginable. Benjamin Githara Karugu allegedly attempted on three consecutive occasions , and before three witnesses, to seize the firearm of the complainant's security officer during a confrontation at Kiamara Estate. The matter was reported to the police. If substantiated, such conduct raises grave questions about the safety of complainants and witnesses involved in criminal proceedings. T he allegations warrant proper investigation , before a murder takes place. What emerges from these controversies is a disturbing picture of how inheritance, corporate ownership and the administration of justice can become battlegrounds where disputed documents and procedural manoeuvres overshadow the search for truth. C onstitutional rights must never become a convenient shield for proven criminal misconduct. Kenya cannot afford a justice system in which disputed signatures determine fortunes, questionable documents reshape ownership, and families spend years struggling to establish the intentions of their deceased relatives. Nor should complainants face intimidation while seeking justice, or investigations be compromised by those entrusted with upholding the law. Perhaps it really is forgery season in Kenya. But seasons eventually end, and when this one does, the true measure of justice will be whether the guilty are held accountable, the innocent are vindicated, and the integrity of the legal system survives the assault. The dead cannot defend their signatures. Let those who are laughing at the graves of those they are trying to defraud continue laughing. When one of the suspects makes a full confession as sources indicate, the laughter will stop.

title: Technical skills offer youth a path from talent to enterprise
description: In a country where formal jobs are scarce, a practical skill remains the most reliable route from unemployment to self-reliance. By Stephen Githinji Technical skills are quietly building the futures that formal employment has failed to deliver for Kenya’s young people. Across barber shops, garages, welding workshops, beauty salons and construction sites, practical training is proving more bankable than a certificate gathering dust while its holder waits for a job that may never come. The journey starts with honest self-knowledge — understanding what you are good at, what problems you can solve and where your curiosity naturally pulls you. Passion rarely arrives with a syllabus. It begins with interest and the courage to start. But talent alone is not enough. Discipline, punctuality and consistency determine whether a skill becomes a sustainable livelihood. A barber who opens two hours late loses clients. A welder who delivers poor work loses the next job. Trustworthiness is not a soft skill — it is the foundation of every lasting business relationship. Professionalism extends to how pressure is handled. Mistakes are inevitable in every trade; what separates the skilled from the struggling is the ability to respond calmly, take responsibility and improve. Customer care matters equally — clients remember how they were treated long after they forget the price. Business literacy converts skill into enterprise. Understanding working capital, mobile payments and simple record-keeping transforms a one-person operation into something that can grow, employ others and endure. The future belongs not to those who wait for opportunity, but to those who build it with their hands. title: Understanding endometriosis: More than just period pain
description: A chronic condition affecting 190 million women worldwide is still taking over a decade to diagnose — and the silence around it is making things worse. By Emmanuel Oltetia Endometriosis affects roughly ten per cent of women and girls of reproductive age globally — approximately 190 million people — yet diagnosis is routinely delayed by between four and twelve years, leaving patients to endure years of suffering that could, with better awareness and faster clinical pathways, be significantly reduced. It is one of the most prevalent chronic conditions on earth, and one of the most poorly understood. The condition occurs when tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus. Because this misplaced tissue responds to the same hormonal cycles as the uterus itself, it bleeds internally, triggering inflammation, scarring and adhesions that can affect the bowel, bladder and broader reproductive function. The hallmark symptoms — debilitating menstrual cramps, chronic pelvic pain, pain during intercourse and heavy bleeding — are frequently dismissed as ordinary period discomfort, which is precisely why so many cases go undetected for so long. Anxiety and depression are common secondary effects. Some individuals, complicating matters further, remain entirely asymptomatic. There is currently no cure. Management focuses on controlling symptoms through non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, hormonal contraceptives to suppress lesion growth, or laparoscopic surgery when medication proves insufficient. Recurrence after surgery remains a persistent challenge, and hysterectomy offers no guarantee of resolution. What is guaranteed is this: the longer diagnosis is delayed, the greater the damage — physical, psychological and reproductive. Endometriosis is not a footnote in women’s health. It is a crisis hiding in plain sight. The post Understanding endometriosis: More than just period pain appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Kenya’s 2027 election crisis: Kalonzo takes opposition case to Washington as IEBC independence comes under fire
description: A high-level opposition delegation has carried Kenya’s deepening electoral anxiety to one of the world’s most influential foreign policy institutions, warning that the conditions for a free and fair vote do not yet exist. By David Kimani Wiper Democratic Movement leader Kalonzo Musyoka has taken Kenya’s pre-election tensions to Washington, leading a senior opposition delegation that met the Council on Foreign Relations on Monday to raise urgent concerns about the independence of the electoral commission, the deployment of state resources for political campaigning, and what the opposition describes as a pattern of organised violence against their supporters. The meeting, which Musyoka confirmed on his official X account, included People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua, former National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi, Ford Kenya’s Eugene Wamalwa, and National Assembly Deputy Minority Leader Robert Mbui. The Council on Foreign Relations was represented by its president, Michael Froman. The delegation’s decision to engage one of Washington’s most respected foreign policy institutions — whose membership includes serving and former heads of state, senior diplomats and leading academics — signals that Kenya’s opposition is internationalising its concerns about the 2027 General Election with deliberate urgency, more than eight months before polling day. At the centre of the opposition’s case is the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission. “There can be no free and fair election when the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission is not independent,” Musyoka wrote in his account of the meeting, a formulation that goes to the heart of Kenya’s recurring post-election disputes. The IEBC has been without a full complement of commissioners since the resignations that followed the 2022 election, and the process of reconstituting the commission has itself become politically charged, with opposition parties accusing the government of seeking to install a compliant body ahead of a consequential election. The opposition’s concerns extend well beyond the composition of the commission. Musyoka and his colleagues told the Council that state funds and civil servants are being deployed for public campaigning on behalf of the ruling administration — a practice that, if substantiated, would constitute a direct violation of Kenya’s electoral laws, which prohibit the use of public resources for partisan purposes. The allegation, which the government has not publicly addressed in response to this specific meeting, reflects a broader anxiety about the uneven playing field that has characterised Kenyan elections across multiple cycles. The violence claims are the most serious element of the opposition’s Washington briefing. Musyoka described a pattern of organised attacks on opposition events: supporters stoned and tear-gassed, vehicles attacked, staff seriously injured and, most gravely, police firing live ammunition. “A regime that turns violence on citizens exercising their democratic rights has no business talking about peaceful elections,” he said. These are allegations that carry significant weight internationally, particularly in the context of Kenya’s history with election-related violence. Independent verification of the specific incidents cited was not immediately available, and the government has not responded publicly to this account of the CFR meeting. The delegation also raised what it characterised as the capture of Parliament by the Executive, arguing that the legislature has been reduced to a rubber stamp and can no longer perform its constitutional function of checking executive power. This is not a new criticism — opposition and civil society voices have repeatedly raised concerns about the relationship between the Ruto administration and the National Assembly — but its presentation to an institution of the Council on Foreign Relations’ standing gives it a new international dimension. Kenya’s foreign policy came under separate scrutiny in the Washington meeting. The opposition drew attention to what it described as President William Ruto’s entanglement with the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan — a paramilitary group that has been accused of mass atrocities in the ongoing Sudanese conflict — and argued that this association has compromised Kenya’s historic reputation as a neutral regional mediator. Kenya’s foreign policy positioning on Sudan has drawn scrutiny from regional analysts, though the government has maintained that its engagement is oriented towards peace facilitation. Underlying all of these concerns is the opposition’s characterisation of corruption under the current administration as having reached levels the country has not previously experienced. “Corruption under Ruto has reached levels this country has never seen, and the rule of law is treated as an inconvenience to be ignored,” Musyoka said. These are claims that the government rejects. The administration has pointed to various anti-corruption initiatives and infrastructure programmes as evidence of responsible governance. The political landscape heading into August 2027 is exceptionally complex. Kenya has never held a genuinely peaceful and uncontested election in which the loser accepted the result without significant dispute. The 2007 post-election violence, the contested results of 2017 and the tight margin of 2022 — which produced a Supreme Court petition before Ruto’s victory was confirmed — have embedded deep institutional scepticism about electoral processes across the political spectrum. What distinguishes the current moment is the scale and sophistication of the opposition’s international engagement. The decision to brief the Council on Foreign Relations, an institution whose analysis shapes American foreign policy thinking, is a deliberate signal that Kenya’s opposition intends to hold its concerns before international audiences throughout the campaign period. The United States, as Kenya’s most significant bilateral partner and a major source of investment and diplomatic support, is not an incidental audience. Whether the CFR meeting produces any concrete response — increased international monitoring commitments, diplomatic pressure around IEBC reconstitution, or formal statements on electoral conditions — remains to be seen. What is already clear is that Kenya’s 2027 election has acquired an international dimension that will be difficult to contain within the country’s borders. The ballot, as Musyoka framed it, is where the opposition intends to settle matters. The question is whether, by the time August arrives, the conditions for a credible vote will have been established. title: McCarthy turns his back on Bafana Bafana to fire Kenya’s Afcon charge
description: The Kenya head coach says his heart belongs entirely to the Harambee Stars as he prepares to face his home country in a crucial Afcon 2027 qualifier tomorrow. By Martin Weche Harambee Stars head coach Benni McCarthy has declared that he feels no sentimentality whatsoever about facing South Africa when Kenya host Bafana Bafana at Nyayo Stadium tomorrow evening in a pivotal Africa Cup of Nations 2027 Group C qualifier. The South African-born coach, who remains his country’s all-time leading scorer, was unequivocal in stating where his loyalties lie. “Nothing to do with me. My passport is South Africa, but I have no say in what they do. With all my experience, everything that I know, my heart goes into giving the best to Kenya national team — and the rest will sort itself out,” McCarthy said. It is a remarkable position for a man who, by any measure, is a giant of South African football. McCarthy, 49, scored 31 goals in 80 international appearances for Bafana Bafana — a record that still stands — and was the focal point of the South African attack across two Fifa World Cup campaigns, netting at both the 1998 tournament in France and the 2002 edition in Japan and South Korea. His most iconic moment in a Bafana shirt came at the 1998 Africa Cup of Nations in Burkina Faso, where he scored four goals in a single 13-minute spell against Namibia and announced himself to the world as one of the continent’s most lethal finishers. The Porto striker he was then bears little relation to the man now plotting South Africa’s downfall from the Kenyan dugout — but the competitive fire, those who know him well insist, has not dimmed one degree. Kenya arrive at tomorrow’s match in a position of unique comfort. As co-hosts of Afcon 2027, alongside Uganda and Tanzania, the Harambee Stars are already guaranteed a place at the continental showpiece regardless of their qualifying results. That assurance has not, however, diluted McCarthy’s ambitions for the group stage. With three matches remaining and nine points still available, he has set a clear target. “We’ve got three matches, there’s nine points still at hand. Our goal is to go for all nine points starting tomorrow. It has no sentimental value for me. This is my job and I give everything for the job that I am in and it is with Kenya,” he said. The backdrop to tomorrow’s fixture is Friday’s 2–2 draw in Soweto, a result that left South Africa frustrated after twice allowing Kenya to peg them back. McCarthy knows Pitso Mosimane’s side will arrive at Nyayo carrying a point to prove. “I know they have quality and they believe that they should be on top — and they are on top of the group. So at the end of the day, it depends on them. They play as many games as we do,” he said, his words carrying the measured confidence of a coach who has studied his opponents carefully and found them beatable. Mosimane, himself a figure of enormous stature in African football, faces the peculiar task of overturning a result against a team managed by one of his country’s most celebrated footballers. The tactical contest between two coaches of this calibre gives tomorrow’s tie a dimension that extends well beyond the Group C standings. Elsewhere in the group, Guinea defeated Eritrea 3–1 in Cairo yesterday, a result that tightens the race for qualification. Bafana Bafana currently lead the group, and a defeat in Nairobi would significantly damage their Afcon ambitions. The stakes, then, are entirely asymmetric — South Africa need a result; Kenya want one for pride and momentum. Kick-off at Nyayo Stadium is set for 7pm, and a capacity crowd is expected to create the kind of atmosphere that McCarthy, in his playing days, would have relished as an opponent. Tomorrow evening, it will be working in his favour. South Africa produced McCarthy the footballer. Kenya, he has made clear, will have everything McCarthy the coach has to give. title: Ten-man England silence Madrid as Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run ends
description: Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White put England three goals up before a red card sparked a Spanish fightback that goalkeeper James Trafford ultimately repelled to seal a famous Nations League victory. By Andalo Christine Ingutia England defeated Spain 3–2 in a stunning UEFA Nations League clash at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid yesterday, ending the hosts’ extraordinary 43-match unbeaten run and finishing top of Group A3 despite playing the final half-hour with ten men. Thomas Tuchel’s side produced a performance of genuine attacking quality and hard-won defensive resilience, surging into a commanding three-goal lead before a red card handed Spain the momentum they needed for a tense, nerve-shredding finale. The result, achieved on Spanish soil against a side that had not lost since March 2024, will rank among England’s finest away performances in recent memory. Both nations finished the group stage on 15 points from six matches, but England claimed top spot on goal difference — +13 against Spain’s +8 — confirming their status as the group’s dominant force. England started with intent, pressing Spain high and creating several promising chances before the hosts settled into their characteristic possession-based rhythm and began to push the visitors back. The breakthrough, when it came, arrived at the perfect moment. In the 45th minute, captain Harry Kane was fouled inside the penalty area by Pau Cubarsí, and Kane stepped up to convert the spot-kick himself, sending England into the interval with a deserved lead and the away end in full voice. The second half began where the first had ended. England returned from the dressing room with renewed purpose and doubled their advantage in the 53rd minute when Ezri Konsa rose above the Spanish defence to head home with authority. Four minutes later, the tie appeared all but settled. Ben White completed a beautifully worked move involving Kane and Jude Bellingham to make it 3–0, and England’s travelling supporters allowed themselves to dream of something historic. Then came the moment that turned the evening on its head. In the 63rd minute, Elliot Anderson was shown a straight red card for pulling back Lamine Yamal as the teenage Spanish winger threatened to break clear on goal. Spain sensed their opening almost immediately. Mikel Oyarzabal stepped forward to convert the resulting penalty in the 65th minute, reducing the deficit to 3–1 and setting the stadium alight. The home side pressed with increasing urgency, and their persistence was rewarded in the 75th minute. Yamal delivered a dangerous delivery across the England defence, and substitute Nico Williams arrived at the far post to finish and make it 3–2. With 15 minutes remaining and Spain in full control of the momentum, the outcome suddenly felt far from certain. What followed was a defensive rearguard of genuine character. England’s back line held its shape under wave after wave of Spanish attack, and goalkeeper James Trafford emerged as the night’s most important figure in an England shirt. The 22-year-old produced a string of vital saves as Spain threw everything forward, commanding his area with a composure that belied his relatively limited international experience. The defining moment came deep in stoppage time. With Spain pressing desperately for an equaliser, Trafford produced a crucial double save to deny Fermín López and preserve England’s slender advantage. When the final whistle sounded, the relief and elation on the England bench was unmistakable. For Spain, defeat ends a streak that had come to feel almost permanent. Luis de la Fuente’s side were not without credit — their second-half response demonstrated exactly why they remain European champions — and they progress to the Nations League quarter-finals as group runners-up. But the manner of this defeat, at home, against ten men, will sting. For England, it is a statement. Tuchel’s side showed they can defend a lead under the most intense pressure, score goals from multiple sources, and find a way to win on the grandest stages. The road to the 2027 World Cup just got a little more interesting. The post Ten-man England silence Madrid as Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run ends appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Gachagua opens DCP’s Nairobi office and vows free nominations ahead of 2027 polls
description: The Democracy for the Citizens Party leader used yesterday’s Nairobi launch to signal grassroots intent, promising smart-card membership, open nominations and no favoured candidates. By James Mwangi Rigathi Gachagua, leader of the Democracy for the Citizens Party, yesterday officially opened the party’s Nairobi County office, using the occasion to announce plans for a smart-card membership system and to pledge that the party’s 2027 nominations would be open, competitive and free of preferential treatment for any aspirant. The launch, held at a party meeting in Nairobi, marked the latest step in DCP’s accelerating effort to build a credible organisational presence in the capital ahead of what is shaping up to be one of Kenya’s most consequential general elections. “The DCP party will hold free and fair nominations, with smart cards for party members to be introduced soon,” Gachagua told those gathered. “There are no special individuals or favoured aspirants. I encourage all aspirants across the country to put their best foot forward and strengthen their grassroots networks ahead of the nominations in March.” The opening of a dedicated Nairobi County office carries significance beyond the symbolic. Nairobi is Kenya’s most populous county and its most politically volatile, a battleground where no single party has historically commanded undisputed loyalty and where the urban vote has repeatedly proven decisive in shaping national outcomes. For DCP, which has built its strongest foundations in Mount Kenya and Maasailand, establishing a visible institutional footprint in the capital represents a deliberate signal of national ambition. Gachagua was direct about what the new office represents. “Today, I was honoured to officially open our new DCP party office for Nairobi County,” he said. “This office is a statement of our commitment to serving Kenyans and strengthening our grassroots presence across the county and the country. We must continue listening to the people and acting on their wishes, as enshrined in Chapter One of the Constitution of Kenya: all sovereign power belongs to the people.” His remarks on party growth carried the confidence of a leader who believes the political tide is running in his direction. “Our party is the party of the moment and the future. We are growing every single day as we work to earn the mandate of the great people of Kenya,” he said, closing with a phrase that has become something of a DCP rallying call: “Green is wealth. Green is the future.” The timing of the Nairobi launch is not incidental. With the IEBC’s published electoral calendar placing party primary nominations between 17 March and 10 April 2027, and membership list submissions required by 16 March, the window for organisational preparation is narrowing faster than many in the political class appear to have fully absorbed. Gachagua’s announcement of a smart-card membership system — a move that would give DCP a verifiable, digitalised record of its membership base — suggests the party is thinking carefully about the administrative requirements of a credible nomination process, not merely the political theatre of rallies and launches. DCP has grown rapidly since its establishment. The party currently has three elected Members of County Assembly and one Member of Parliament among its ranks, and has attracted figures of political weight from both the Mount Kenya and Maasailand regions. It is widely regarded as one of the most consequential new political forces heading into 2027, with Gachagua himself described by analysts as a potential kingmaker whose endorsement could prove structurally decisive for any presidential candidate seeking a majority. The question of whether Gachagua will seek the presidency himself or transfer his support to another candidate — including DCP Secretary-General John Methu, whose name he has previously floated — remains publicly unresolved. Yesterday’s event offered no fresh clarity on that front. What it did offer was a portrait of a party leader investing seriously in the machinery of political organisation: offices, membership systems, open nominations and a constitutional framing of popular sovereignty that speaks to voters wary of elite deal-making. Whether DCP can translate that organisational investment into electoral dominance across a city as complex and competitive as Nairobi will be one of the defining tests of the party’s national credibility in the months ahead. title: Later: The quiet procrastination of a day off and the book that waited until evening
description: A day off, a book within reach and the small, familiar voice that keeps saying there is still time — until there almost isn’t. By Munavvar Tlewbaeva Procrastination rarely announces itself — it arrives quietly, dressed as good intention, and spends the day rearranging the furniture of your plans until evening falls and you realise the thing you most wanted to do is still exactly where you left it that morning. That was the shape of one particular day off: a book on the table, work that needed finishing, and the easy promise made to oneself that one would follow the other. It had seemed so simple when the day began. Wake up, finish the outstanding work — there was not much of it — and then settle in with the book that had been waiting. That was all. No grand ambitions, no complicated schedule. Just a few hours of quiet reading on a day that belonged, for once, entirely to oneself. Work came first. That much was reasonable. Hands busy, thoughts wandering, the morning moved forward in the way mornings do when you are half-present. At some point, almost without deciding to, the phone appeared and Chingiz Aitmatov’s The First Teacher began to play — an audiobook, a voice in the background, something to fill the silence while the hands kept moving. At first it was barely there, a murmur beneath the thoughts. Then a sentence caught the attention. Then another. The pace of work slowed imperceptibly, not enough to notice, just enough for the story to find its way in. There is something particular about listening to a great writer while doing something ordinary. The words arrive without effort, without the conscious act of sitting down and opening a page, and perhaps because of that they carry a different kind of weight. Aitmatov’s Central Asian plains and the fierce simplicity of his characters settled over the room like afternoon light. The work continued. The listening deepened. And still the book on the table went untouched. This is the texture of so many days — not dramatic, not marked by any visible failure, but quietly shaped by the gap between what we intended and what we actually did. The tea gets drunk. The window gets glanced at. The list of things still to do gets mentally revised and silently carried forward. From the outside, nothing has changed. From the inside, the day is slowly becoming something other than what was planned. By the time the work was done — most of it, at least — the afternoon had given way to early evening. The recording was still playing. The book lay where it had been since morning, two steps away, untouched. Not because there had been no time. Not because anything had prevented it. Simply because the moment had never quite felt right, and the moment that never quite feels right has a way of persisting until the light outside changes colour. It would be easy, at this point, to reach for self-reproach. But that impulse deserves a little scrutiny. People do not always leave things undone because they are careless or idle. Sometimes they are genuinely tired. Sometimes the small reserves of energy that remain after work and obligation are not quite enough to begin something new, even something deeply wanted. And sometimes — perhaps most honestly — there is the assumption of tomorrow: the quiet, largely unexamined belief that the time will come, that the book will be read, that the moment will arrive when everything feels right for it. That assumption has a long history of being wrong. The recording reached its end. The street outside had grown dark and quieter. The day off was nearly over. The book was still on the table. It took no great act of will to pick it up. It never does. It was two steps away. The cover opened. The first page appeared. The first line was read. Then a pause. The clock on the wall. Not too late — not quite. Outside, tomorrow was waiting, as it always seems to be. The book lay open. The first line had been read. Whether the second followed is, perhaps, beside the point. Munavvar Tlewbaeva is a fourth-year student at the Chimbay Faculty of Karakalpak State University, Uzbekistan.
